Mint marks: D, S . Found immediately above the date on the obverse. Philadelphia Mint specimens lack mint mark. W (2009)
Design: Liberty holding a torch and olive branch, backed by the rays of the Sun, the U.S. Capitol visible; 46 stars circle design

sents: lead
The Saint-Gaudens double eagle is a twenty- dollar gold coin, or double eagle, produced by the United States Mint from 1907 to 1933.
lead
The coin is named after its designer, the sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, who designed the obverse and reverse.
lead
It is considered by many to be the most beautiful of U.S. coins.
lead
In 1904, President Theodore Roosevelt sought to beautify American coinage, and proposed Saint-Gaudens as an artist capable of the task.
lead
Although the sculptor had poor experiences with the Mint and its chief engraver, Charles E.
lead
Barber, Saint-Gaudens accepted Roosevelt's call.
lead
The work was subject to considerable delays, due to Saint-Gaudens's declining health and difficulties because of the high relief of his design.
lead
Saint-Gaudens died in 1907, after designing the eagle and double eagle, but before the designs were finalized for production.
Background

The double eagle, or twenty-dollar gold piece, was first issued in 1850; its congressional authorization was a response to the increasing amount of gold available as the result of the California Gold Rush.
Background
The resulting Liberty Head double eagle, designed by Mint Engraver James Longacre, was struck for the remainder of the 19th century, though the design was modified several times.
Background

The double eagle, due to its very high face value, equivalent to several hundred dollars today, did not widely circulate, but was the coin most often used for large international transactions, in which settlement was to be in gold.
Background
Sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens's first association with the Mint was in 1891, when he served on a committee judging entries for the new silver coinage.
Background
The Mint had offered only a small prize to the winner, and all invited artists (including Saint-Gaudens himself) refused to submit entries.
Background
Leech that there were only four men in the world capable of such work, of whom three were in France and Saint-Gaudens was the fourth.
Background
Barber, who had been Chief Engraver since 1879, felt that Saint-Gaudens overstated the case, and there was only one man capable of such coinage work—Barber himself.
Background
In 1892, Saint-Gaudens was asked to design the official medal of the World Columbian Exposition in Chicago; it would be presented to prizewinning exhibitors.
Background
The exposition directors hastily withdrew the reverse design and replaced it with one created by Barber which, according to numismatic historian Walter Breen, was "notable only for banality".
Background
A furious Saint-Gaudens swore to have nothing more to do with the Mint or its employees, and for the next decade refused all commissions which might involve him with that bureau.
Inception

On December 27, 1904, President Theodore Roosevelt, a personal friend of Saint-Gaudens, wrote to his Secretary of the Treasury, Leslie Mortier Shaw: "I think the state of our coinage is artistically of atrocious hideousness.
Inception
In November 1905, Roosevelt wrote to Saint-Gaudens to enquire how the gold coinage was progressing.
Inception
The President mentioned that he had been looking at gold coins of Ancient Greece, and that the most beautiful ones were in high relief.
Inception
On January 2, 1906, Saint-Gaudens wrote to Shaw, enquiring whether a high relief was practical on coins struck at the Mint.
Inception
In May 1906, the sculptor wrote to Roosevelt that he had sent an assistant to Washington to obtain the technical details of the redesign, but "if you succeed in getting the best of the polite Mr.
Inception
In May 1906, Saint-Gaudens wrote to Secretary Shaw, asking if there was any objection to having the date in Roman numerals.
Inception

I have reminded our architects that I will dismiss the first one who puts a V on a public building where a U is intended." However, Roosevelt overruled Shaw, and the sculptor proceeded with the use of Roman numerals.
Inception
Saint-Gaudens's health worsened through 1906, as the cancer which would kill him forced him to have his assistant, Henry Hering, deal with many of the details of the work.
Inception
The figure is surrounded by 46 stars, one for each of the states in 1907.
From design to coin

At that time, the Mint was intensely busy generating designs for new coinage for Cuba and the Philippines, and Barber was reluctant to waste time on what he considered an experimental piece which would never be coined for circulation.
From design to coin
Approximately 24 pieces were struck as patterns; even though the Mint used a medal press, set for maximum pressure, it still took up to nine strokes of the press to fully bring out the design.
From design to coin
These patterns are today known as the "Ultra High Relief" or "Extra High Relief" pieces, and only about 20 are known —one sold in a 2005 auction for $2,990,000.
From design to coin

On May 8, 1907, the President wrote Saint-Gaudens, "It has proved hitherto impossible to strike them by one blow, which is necessary under the conditions of making coins of the present day." On May 11, 1907, Saint-Gaudens replied, "I am grieved that the striking of the die did not bring better results.
From design to coin

Saint-Gaudens had produced the models for these dies under the misapprehension that the first pieces had been struck on a production press, rather than on the Mint's only medal press, and therefore only slight adjustment need be made.
From design to coin
When Saint-Gaudens died on August 3, 1907, Hering was working on a third model.
From design to coin
Uncertain where to find Hering, Roosevelt ordered the new Secretary of the Treasury, George Cortelyou, to have the Mint finalize the design and put the coin in circulation by September 1.
From design to coin
Barber was recalled from his vacation in Ocean Grove, New Jersey, to comply with the President's order.
From design to coin

Barber wrote Philadelphia Mint Superintendent John Landis on August 14 that what Roosevelt wanted was impossible; he had no dies nor any clear idea of how Saint-Gaudens had planned to reduce the relief.
From design to coin
On September 28, Hering finally appeared at the Mint with a new set of models, which Barber again quickly rejected.
From design to coin
In August 1907, Roosevelt nominated San Francisco Mint Superintendent Frank Leach as Director of the Mint; he took office on November 1, 1907.
From design to coin

On November 18, the impatient Roosevelt directed that the second set of dies be used to strike coins, directly ordering the Mint to "begin the new issue, even if it takes you all day to strike one piece!" Over 12,000 of these "High Relief" pieces were struck and were released into circulation in 1907 and 1908.
From design to coin
A total of 361,667 of the revised design were produced by the Mint in 1907; the "Low Relief" coins were released into circulation at the end of December 1907.
From design to coin
Among other alterations, Barber changed the Roman numeral MCMVII for the date to the Arabic numeral "1907".
From design to coin
Yeoman in his A Guide Book of United States Coins, many consider the Saint-Gaudens double eagles the most beautiful of U.S. coins.
From design to coin
Responsibility for most of the delays in producing the new coinage must fall on the Saint-Gaudens studio for failing to deliver models in a timely manner.
From design to coin

Mint Director Leach recalled that when "I laid upon his desk a sample of beautifully executed double eagles of the Saint-Gaudens design, he was most enthusiastic in his expressions of pleasure and satisfaction.
Production
In 1912, two more stars were added to the obverse to reflect the admission of New Mexico and Arizona to the Union.
Production
The only major variety of the series occurred in 1909, an overdate in which an 8 shows under the final nine in the date.
Production
This most likely happened when a 1908 die was struck by a 1909-dated hub, creating the overdate.
Production
Perhaps half of the 161,282 double eagles struck at Philadelphia that year display the overdate.
Production
In 1916, minting of double eagles ceased, as bullion prices were rising because of World War I, which also caused an influx of American gold coins from Europe.
Production
Holders of gold coin, such as banks, refused to pay them out at par value, and they vanished from circulation.
Production
The coin was struck in large numbers once coinage was resumed in 1920, but it was now almost exclusively a coin of international trade, or was held by banks as backing for gold certificates.
Production
The onset of the Depression in 1929 did not halt the minting of double eagles, but the coins were for the most part held in Treasury vaults, and few were released.
Production
Despite a mintage of almost 1.8 million pieces of the 1929 double eagle, it is estimated that fewer than 2,000 exist today, with all the rest melted by the government in the late 1930s.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
According to numismatic historian Roger Burdette, the first 1933 double eagles were struck on March 2, 1933.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
On March 15, 1933, 25,000 new double eagles were delivered to Mint Cashier Harry Powell, and by longstanding Mint custom, were available for paying out.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle

On March 6, however, the newly inaugurated president, Franklin Roosevelt, had ordered the Treasury not to pay out any gold, and ordered that banks holding gold transmit it to their Federal Reserve bank.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
On December 28, 1933, Acting Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau ordered Americans to turn in all gold coins and gold certificates, with limited exceptions, receiving paper money in payment.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
Millions of gold coins were melted down by the Treasury in the following years.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
Two 1933 double eagles were sent by the Mint to the Smithsonian Institution for the National Coin Collection, where they remain today.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
David Bowers suggests that despite the ban on paying out gold, examples of the 1933 double eagle could have been obtained legally from Mint Cashier Powell in an exchange for earlier double eagles.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
Dealer William Nagy later recalled visiting Secretary Woodin and being shown five 1933 double eagles, with the secretary stating that he had several more.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
By the early 1940s, between eight and ten specimens were known; two of them were sold by Texas dealer B.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
In 1944, a journalist enquired of the Mint regarding the 1933 double eagles.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
Mint officials could find no record of any issuance of the coins, and decided those in private hands must have been obtained illegally.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
Over the next few years, the Secret Service seized a number of specimens, which were subsequently melted.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
What became of the Farouk specimen after his death is unclear, but the coin resurfaced in the late 1990s.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
In 2002 this coin sold at auction by Sotheby's for $7,590,020.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
The purchase price included $20 paid to the federal government to monetize a coin it contended had never been officially released.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
It sold again in 2021 for $18.9 million.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
In 2004, 10 specimens of the 1933 double eagle were submitted to the Mint for authentication by the heirs of a Philadelphia jeweler who may have been involved in obtaining them from the Mint in 1933.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
The Mint authenticated them, and refused to give them back.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
The heirs brought suit against the government in 2006, and a federal judge ordered the government to file a forfeiture action regarding the coins.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
The government brought such a suit in 2009; it was tried in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania beginning on July 7, 2011.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
On July 21, 2011, a jury decided that the coins had been properly seized by the Federal government.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
Davis confirmed that jury verdict on August 29, 2012.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle

On April 17, 2015, a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled that the government had failed to file its forfeiture action in a timely manner, and that the heirs were entitled to the coins.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
That ruling was vacated by the full court on July 28, 2015, and the case set for further argument.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
On August 1, 2016, the full Third Circuit ruled in favor of the government, upholding the jury verdict.
End of the series; the 1933 double eagle
The heirs, on November 4 of that year, asked the Supreme Court to review the case, which refused to hear it on April 21, 2017, ending the case.
Reuse of the design
The obverse has appeared on American gold bullion coinage issued since 1986.
Reuse of the design
Saint-Gaudens's original design was reused, with two stars added next to the two which Barber had added in 1912, recognizing the admission of Alaska and Hawaii to the Union.
Reuse of the design
In 1907, the Mint had experimented by striking about two dozen pieces of the same weight as the double eagle, bearing Saint-Gaudens's design, but which had a smaller, thicker planchet.
Reuse of the design
In 2009, the Mint struck a similar piece in.999 gold, using Saint-Gaudens's original ultra high relief design for both sides of the coin, though modified to a 50-star obverse.
Mintages and rarity
Note: The 2009 Ultra High Relief was minted in the West Point Mint, but has no mint mark.
Mintages and rarity
Coins remaining in bank vaults in the United States were melted after 1933; coins in bank vaults overseas were not.
Mintages and rarity

By way of example, the 1924 Saint-Gaudens double eagle was once thought to be rare although 4,323,500 were struck; when the Mint offered a list of coins available at face value plus postage in 1932, the 1924 was not on that list.
Mintages and rarity
Large quantities of 1924 double eagles were found in European bank vaults, and today the 1924 is one of the most common of the series.
Mintages and rarity
On the other hand, the 1925-S had 3,776,500 struck, but few were released or exported, remaining in Treasury and bank vaults—but available from the Treasury at face value in 1932.
Mintages and rarity
Fewer than a thousand are known to have survived; one, in almost-perfect condition (graded MS -67) sold in 2005 for $287,500.

The Flowing Hair dollar was the first dollar coin issued by the United States federal government.
lead
The coin was minted in 1794 and 1795; its size and weight were based on the Spanish dollar, which was popular in trade throughout the Americas.
lead
In 1791, following a study by Alexander Hamilton, Congress passed a joint resolution calling for the establishment of a national mint.
lead
Later that year, in his third State of the Union address, President George Washington urged Congress to provide for a mint, which was officially authorized by the Coinage Act of 1792.
lead
Despite the authorization, silver and gold coins were not struck until 1794.
lead
The Flowing Hair dollar, designed by Robert Scot, was initially produced in 1794, and again in 1795.
Background

In 1789, the United States Constitution, which granted Congress the power "to coin Money, regulate the Value thereof, and of foreign Coin, and fix the Standard of Weights and Measures", was ratified and came into force.
Background

On January 28, 1791, Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton presented a report to Congress detailing the findings of a study he had conducted on the monetary system and the potential of a United States mint.
Background
Hamilton's recommendation was that the dollar should contain 371.25 grains of silver and have a gross weight of 416 grains, the balance being copper.
Background
On March 3, 1791, after reviewing Hamilton's report, Congress passed a joint resolution authorizing a federal mint; the resolution, however, gave no specifics or appropriations.
Establishment of the Mint
Measures have been taken pursuant to that resolution for procuring some of the most necessary artists, together with the requisite apparatus.
Establishment of the Mint

The committee presented a bill before Congress on December 21, 1791, which stated in part that the new dollar coin (which was to form the basis of the United States monetary system) should contain 371 grains of silver and a total weight of 416 grains, as Hamilton had earlier recommended.
Establishment of the Mint
The new silver coins were to be struck in an alloy containing 1,485 parts out of 1,664 (about 89.24 percent) fine silver, with the remainder copper, intended to equal the silver in Spanish dollars.
Establishment of the Mint
However, an assay of the Spanish dollars was in error—they were in fact 65/72 silver (about 90.28 percent) with the remainder copper.
Establishment of the Mint
The law, known as the Coinage Act of 1792, was signed into law on April 2, 1792, by President Washington.
Establishment of the Mint
On July 31, 1792, the foundation stone of the Philadelphia Mint was laid by newly appointed Mint Director David Rittenhouse.
Establishment of the Mint
Machinery and personnel began occupying the new building by September 1792, and production began on cents in February 1793.
Establishment of the Mint
On March 3, 1794, Congress lowered the bonds to $5,000 and $1,000 for chief coiner and assayer, respectively.
Design creation
Early in 1794, engraver Robert Scot began preparing designs for the silver dollar.
Design creation
Scot's initial design depicted a bust of Liberty, while his reverse featured an eagle, both required by the 1792 Coinage Act.
Design creation
Extra care was taken during the engraving of this denomination, because the dollar would be the largest American coin, and would thus receive the most scrutiny from foreign nations.
Minting

After receiving several deposits, assayer Albion Cox notified Rittenhouse of his beliefs that the.892 standard approved for silver coinage was difficult to produce and that it would darken if put into circulation.
Minting
Instead, Cox recommended that the purity be modified to.900 fine, but also that the weight be kept at 416 grains.
Minting
The Mint's action cost suppliers of silver about one percent of their deposit; the largest depositor, John Vaughan, reckoned his loss at $2,260.

Minting

The new coinage press was completed in early 1795, and the first group of dollars, totalling 3,810 coins, was delivered on May 6.

The coins struck on May 8 may have borne a 1794 date, however there is no document or evidence to support such a statement.

Minting
The total mintage for the second and final year of production is estimated at 160,295.

The Draped Bust dollar is a United States dollar coin minted from 1795 to 1803, and was reproduced, dated 1804, into the 1850s.
lead
The design succeeded the Flowing Hair dollar, which began mintage in 1794 and was the first silver dollar struck by the United States Mint.
lead
The designer is unknown, though the distinction is usually credited to artist Gilbert Stuart.
lead
The model is also unknown, though Ann Willing Bingham has been suggested.
lead

In October 1795, newly appointed Mint Director Elias Boudinot ordered that the legal fineness of 0.892 (89.2%) silver be used for the dollar rather than the unauthorized fineness of 0.900 (90%) silver that had been used since the denomination was first minted in 1794.
lead
Due largely to a decrease in the amount of silver deposited at the Philadelphia Mint, coinage of silver dollars declined throughout the latter years of the 18th century.
lead
In 1804, coinage of silver dollars was halted; the last date used during regular mint production was 1803.
lead
In 1834, silver dollar production was temporarily restarted to supply a diplomatic mission to Asia with a special set of proof coins.
Background
Coinage began on the first United States silver dollar, known as the Flowing Hair dollar, in 1794 following the construction and staffing of the Philadelphia Mint.
Background
The Coinage Act of 1792 called for the silver coinage to be struck in an alloy consisting of 89.2% silver and 10.8% copper.
Background

Julian speculates that Henry William de Saussure, who was named Director of the Mint on July 9, 1795, may have suggested it, as he had stated a redesign of the American coinage as one of his goals before taking office.
Production
Julian, however, places the beginning of production in either late September or early October 1795, while Taxay asserts that the first new silver dollars were struck in October.
Production
In September 1795, de Saussure wrote his resignation letter to President Washington.
Production
Upon assuming his duties at the Mint on October 28, Boudinot was informed of the silver standard that had been used since the first official silver coins were struck.
Production
He immediately ordered that this practice be ceased and that coinage would begin in the 89.2% fineness approved by the Coinage Act of 1792.
Production

Production

Production
Bullion deposits continued to decline, and in 1797, silver dollar production reached the lowest point since 1794 with a mintage of just 7,776 pieces.
Production
During this time, silver deposits declined to such an extent that Thomas Jefferson personally deposited 300 Spanish dollars in June 1797.

Production
Although silver bullion deposits at the Mint had increased, Boudinot attempted to end silver dollar production in 1803, favoring half dollars instead.

cent_1913_liberty_head_nickel.title: 1913 Liberty Head nickel
sents: lead

The 1913 Liberty Head nickel is an American five-cent piece which was produced in extremely limited quantities unauthorized by the United States Mint, making it one of the best-known and most coveted rarities in American numismatics.
lead
In 1972, one specimen of the five cent coin became the first coin to sell for over US$100,000; in 1996, another specimen became the first to sell for over US$1 million.
lead
A specimen was sold for US$3 million in a 2004 private sale, then resold for US$3.7 million at a public auction in 2010.
lead
Only five examples are known to exist: two in private collections and three in museums.
Origin
The Indian Head (Buffalo) nickel was introduced in February 1913, replacing the Liberty Head design.
Origin
These were the first official strikings of nickels in 1913, since the United States Mint 's official records list no Liberty Head nickels produced in that year.
Origin
However, in December, 1919, a previously unknown 1913 Liberty Head nickel was shown at a meeting of the Chicago Coin Club.
Origin

Then in August 1920, the general numismatic community learned of five Liberty Head nickels dated 1913, all owned by Samuel Brown, a numismatist who attended the American Numismatic Association 's annual convention and displayed the coins there.
Origin

He had shown the nickel at the Chicago club meeting and had previously placed an advertisement in the December 1919 issue of The Numismatist soliciting information on these coins, offering to pay US $500 for each and ostensibly purchasing them as a result.
Origin
If true, this was not a unique occurrence; such clandestine strikes were quite common in the 19th century, with the Class II and III 1804 silver dollars perhaps the best-known instance.
Pedigree
In January 1924, Samuel Brown sold all five 1913 Liberty Head nickels.
Pedigree
Green (son of the famous Gilded Age investor Hetty Green), who kept them in his collection until his death in 1936.
Pedigree
Johnson, who broke up the set for the first time.
Pedigree
Later rumors that there is a sixth specimen that was lost or is otherwise hidden appear to be unfounded.
Eliasberg specimen
Of the five 1913 Liberty Head nickels, two have proof surfaces and the other three were produced with standard striking techniques.
Eliasberg specimen
The Eliasberg specimen is the finest known 1913 Liberty Head nickel, with a grade of 66 from various professional grading services, including PCGS and NGC.
Eliasberg specimen
In May 1996, it was sold at an auction conducted by Bowers and Merena to rarities dealer Jay Parrino for US$1,485,000: the highest price for a coin up until that point.
Eliasberg specimen
When it was auctioned again in March 2001, the price climbed to US$1,840,000.
Eliasberg specimen
In May 2005, Legend Numismatics purchased the Eliasberg specimen for US$4,150,000.
Eliasberg specimen
In 2007, it was sold to an unnamed collector in California for US$5 million.
Olsen specimen
While the Eliasberg specimen is the best preserved of the five coins, the Olsen specimen is almost certainly the most famous.
Olsen specimen
It has been graded Proof-64 by both PCGS and NGC, and was featured on an episode of Hawaii Five-O ("The $100,000 Nickel", aired on December 11, 1973).
Olsen specimen
When Newman and Johnson broke up the set of five coins, the Olsen specimen was sold first to James Kelly and then to Fred Olsen.
Olsen specimen
In 1972, it was sold to World Wide Coin Investments for US$100,000, thus inspiring its title appearance in Hawaii Five-O the following year.
Olsen specimen
Its price doubled to US$200,000 when it was resold to Superior Galleries in 1978.
Olsen specimen
It has been resold on several occasions since then, fetching US$3,000,000 in a private treaty sale from California collector Dwight Manley to Bruce Morelan and Legend Numismatics in June 2004.
Olsen specimen
Legend sold the coin to Blanchard and Co. in 2005, who sold it to a private collector, and more recently for US$3,737,500 by Heritage Auctions in January 2010.
Norweb specimen
The Norweb specimen is one of two 1913 Liberty Head nickels that have ended up in museums.
Norweb specimen
In 1949, it was purchased by King Farouk to replace the Olsen specimen, which he had sold.
Norweb specimen
The Norwebs donated the specimen to the Smithsonian Institution’s National Numismatic Collection — where it remains — in 1978 to commemorate their sixtieth wedding anniversary.
Walton specimen
The Walton specimen is the most elusive of the five 1913 Liberty Head nickels; for over 40 years, its whereabouts were unknown and it was believed to have been lost.
Walton specimen
Walton, for whom the specimen is named, purchased it from Newman and Johnson in 1945 for approximately US$3,750, equal to $ 63,466 today.
Walton specimen
On March 9, 1962, Walton died in a car crash en route to a coin show.
Walton specimen
US$250,000 worth of coins were recovered from the crash site, including the 1913 Liberty nickel, which was protected in a custom-made holder.
Walton specimen
When Walton's heirs put his coins up for public auction in 1963, the nickel was returned to them, because the auction house had mistakenly determined the coin to be not genuine.
Walton specimen
As a result, the coin remained in the family's possession, being stored in a strongbox on the floor of a closet in his sister's home, for over 40 years.
Walton specimen
In July 2003, the American Numismatic Association arranged to display the four specimens whose whereabouts were known.
Walton specimen

He arranged with Bowers and Merena auction house (at the time a division of Collectors Universe, Inc.) to offer a minimum US$1 million to purchase the coin, or as a guarantee for consigning it to one of their public auctions.
Walton specimen
In addition, a US$10,000 reward was offered simply for letting representatives of Bowers and Merena be the first to see the missing fifth specimen when found.
Walton specimen
The coin was sold at auction by the heirs in April 2013 for US$3,172,500, significantly above an estimated value of US$2,500,000.
Walton specimen

The auction buyers, Jeff Garrett, (former ANA President) and owner of Mid-American Rare Coin Galleries in Lexington, Kentucky, partnering with esteemed numismatist, Larry Lee, put it on display at Lee’s store, Coin & Bullion Reserves in Panama City, Florida.
Walton specimen
In June 2018 Garrett and Lee sold the 1913 Walton, in a private treaty sale reported to be between $3 and $4 million, to Martin Burns, a lawyer from Las Vegas, and his brother Ron Firman, of Miami.
Walton specimen
The brothers then arranged for the Walton specimen to come back to the ANA museum, where it had stayed beginning in July 2018.
Walton specimen
In October 2022 the Firman family sold the coin to GreatCollections Coin Auctions for US$4,200,000.
McDermott specimen

Held by the American Numismatic Association 's Money Museum in Colorado Springs, Colorado, the McDermott specimen has the distinction of being the only 1913 Liberty Head nickel with circulation marks on it.
McDermott specimen
After his death, the coin was then sold at auction to Aubrey Bebee in 1967 for US$46,000, who along with his wife donated it to the ANA in 1989, where it is exhibited in the Money Museum.

A 1913 Liberty Head nickel is the target of a theft plot by the antagonists in Season 6, Episode 14, of the television series Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series), titled "The $100,000 Nickel."
In popular culture
A 1913 Liberty Head nickel is also featured in the Bernie Rhodenbarr novel "The Burglar Who Studied Spinoza" by Lawrence Block.
In popular culture
A missing 1913 Liberty Head nickel also features prominently in the plot of the 1981 The Hardy Boys book " The Vanishing Thieves ".

sents: lead
The Capped Bust coinage of the United States consisted of a half dime, dime, quarter and half dollar.
History
It proved to be a popular design and lasted from 1807 to 1839 on the half dollar, 1815 to 1838 on the quarter, 1809 to 1837 on the dime, and 1829 to 1837 on the half dime.
History
All four of these coin were struck in 89.2% silver and 10.8% copper.
History

There was also a gold design created by engraver Robert Scot created in 1795, also called the Capped Bust, although it is more popularly known as the " Turban Head " because of its unusual, exotic appearance.
History
The Turban design was used on the gold Quarter Eagle, Half Eagle, and Eagle from 1795 to 1834.
History

On the Quarter and Half Eagles, the Turban design was replaced with the regular Capped Bust design in 1808 and 1807, respectively, while the Eagle, having been out of production since 1804, adopted the "Coronet" Liberty Head design in 1838.
History
The obverse of the 2008 Andrew Jackson's Liberty First Spouse coin and medal features the Capped Bust design.

anct_44_bc_eid_mar_denarius_of_brut.title: Denarius
sents: lead
The denarius (Latin:; pl.: dēnāriī, Latin:) was the standard Roman silver coin from its introduction in the Second Punic War c.
lead
211 BC to the reign of Gordian III (AD 238–244), when it was gradually replaced by the antoninianus.
lead
It continued to be minted in very small quantities, likely for ceremonial purposes, until and through the Tetrarchy (293–313).
lead
The word dēnārius is derived from the Latin dēnī "containing ten", as its value was originally of 10 assēs.
lead
The word for "money" descends from it in Italian (denaro), Slovene (denar), Portuguese (dinheiro), and Spanish (dinero).
lead
Its name also survives in the dinar currency.
lead
Its symbol is represented in Unicode as 𐆖 (U+10196), a numeral monogram that appeared on the obverse in the Republican period, denoting the 10 asses ("X") to 1 denarius ("I") conversion rate.
lead
However it can also be represented as X̶ (capital letter X with combining long stroke overlay).
History
A predecessor of the denarius was first struck in 269 or 268 BC, five years before the First Punic War, with an average weight of 6.81 grams, or 1 ⁄ 48 of a Roman pound.
History
The first distinctively Roman silver coin appeared around 226 BC.
History
This, with a two-horse chariot or biga which was used as a reverse type for some early denarii, was the prototype for the most common designs used on Roman silver coins for a number of years.
History
Rome overhauled its coinage shortly before 211 BC, and introduced the denarius alongside a short-lived denomination called the victoriatus.
History
The denarius contained an average 4.5 grams, or 1 ⁄ 72 of a Roman pound, of silver, and was at first tariffed at ten asses, hence its name, which means 'tenner'.
History
Under the rule of Augustus (27 BC – 14 AD) its weight fell to 3.9 grams (a theoretical weight of 1 ⁄ 84 of a Roman pound).
History
It remained at nearly this weight until the time of Nero (AD 37–68), when it was reduced to 1 ⁄ 96 of a pound, or 3.4 grams.
History
Later Roman emperors also reduced its weight to 3 grams around the late 3rd century.
History
The value at its introduction was 10 asses, giving the denarius its name, which translates as "containing ten".
History
In about 141 BC, it was re-tariffed at 16 asses, to reflect the decrease in weight of the as.
History
The denarius continued to be the main coin of the Roman Empire until it was replaced by the antoninianus in the early 3rd century AD.
History
The coin was last issued, in bronze, under Aurelian between 270 and 275 AD, and in the first years of the reign of Diocletian.
Value, comparisons and silver content
During the republic (509 BC – 27 BC), a legionary earned 112.5 denarii per year (0.3 denarii per day).
Value, comparisons and silver content

Under Julius Caesar, this was doubled to 225 denarii /yr, with soldiers having to pay for their own food and arms, while in the reign of Augustus a Centurion received at least 3,750 denarii per year, and for the highest rank, 15,000 denarii.
Value, comparisons and silver content
27 BC), a common soldier or unskilled laborer would be paid 1 denarius /day (with no tax deductions), around 300% inflation compared to the early period.
Value, comparisons and silver content
Using the cost of bread as a baseline, this pay equates to around US$20 in 2013 terms.
Value, comparisons and silver content
Expressed in terms of the price of silver, and assuming 0.999 purity, a 1 ⁄ 10 troy ounce denarius had a precious metal value of around US$2.60 in 2021.
Value, comparisons and silver content

At the height of the Roman Empire a sextarius (546 ml or about 2 1 ⁄ 4 American cups) of ordinary wine cost roughly one dupondius (1 ⁄ 8 of a denarius); after Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices was issued in 301 AD, the same item cost 8 debased common denarii – 6300% inflation.
Value, comparisons and silver content
Under the Roman Empire (after Nero) the denarius contained approximately 50 grains, 3.24 grams, or 0.105 ozt (about 1 ⁄ 10 troy ounce).
Value, comparisons and silver content
From a purity of greater than 90% silver in the 1st century AD, the denarius fell to under 60% purity by 200 AD, and plummeted to 5% purity by 300 AD.
Influence
In the final years of the 1st century BC Tincomarus, a local ruler in southern Britain, started issuing coins that appear to have been made from melted down denarii.
Influence
The lasting legacy of the denarius can be seen in the use of "d" as the abbreviation for the British penny until 1971.
Influence
The pre-decimal currency of the United Kingdom until 1970 of pounds, shillings and pence was abbreviated as lsd, with "d" referring to denarius and standing for penny.
Use in the Bible
In the New Testament, the gospels refer to the denarius as a day's wage for a common laborer (Matthew 20:2, John 12:5).
Use in the Bible
Thus, in the conditions pictured by Revelation 6, the normal income for a working-class family would buy enough food for only one person.
Use in the Bible
The denarius is also mentioned in the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant & in Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37).
Use in the Bible
The Render unto Caesar passage in Matthew 22:15–22 and Mark 12:13–17 uses the word (δηνάριον) to describe the coin held up by Jesus, translated in the King James Bible as " tribute penny ".

The ruble or rouble (Russian: рубль, romanized: rublʹ; symbol: ₽; abbreviation: руб or р. in Cyrillic, Rub in Latin; ISO code: RUB) is the currency of the Russian Federation.
lead
The ruble is subdivided into 100 kopecks (sometimes written as copeck or kopek; Russian: копе́йка, romanized: kopeyka, pl. копе́йки, kopeyki).
lead
It is used in Russia as well as in the parts of Ukraine under Russian military occupation and in Russian-occupied parts of Georgia.
lead
The ruble was the currency of the Russian Empire and of the Soviet Union (as the Soviet ruble).
lead
In 1992, the currency imagery underwent a redesign as a result of the fall of the Soviet Union.
lead
The first Russian ruble (code: RUR) replaced the Soviet ruble (code: SUR) in September 1993 at par.
lead
On 1 January 1998, preceding the Russian financial crisis, the ruble was redenominated with the new code "RUB" and was exchanged at the rate of 1 RUB = 1,000 RUR.
History
The ruble has been used in the Russian territories since the 14th century, and is the second-oldest currency still in circulation, behind sterling.
History
Initially an uncoined unit of account, the ruble became a circulating coin in 1704 just before the establishment of the Russian Empire.
History
It was also the first currency in Europe to be decimalised in 1704, when it was divided into 100 kopecks.
Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, the Soviet ruble remained the currency of the Russian Federation until 1992.
A new set of coins was issued in 1992 and a new set of banknotes was issued in the name of Bank of Russia in 1993.
The currency replaced the Soviet ruble at par and was assigned the ISO 4217 code RUR and number 810.
RUR coins
After the fall of the Soviet Union, the Russian Federation introduced new coins in 1992 in denominations of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 rubles.

In 2018, the Central Bank issued a 100 ₽ "commemorative" banknote designed to recognize Russia's role as the host of the 2018 World Cup soccer tournament.

Despite the note being intended for legal tender transactions, the Central Bank has simultaneously refused to allow the country's automated teller machines (ATMs) to recognize or accept it.

silv_1870_s_seated_liberty_dollar.title: Seated Liberty dollar

Mint marks: O, S, CC . Located beneath eagle on reverse. Philadelphia Mint specimens lack a mint mark.

sents: lead
The Seated Liberty dollar was a dollar coin struck by the United States Mint from 1840 to 1873 and designed by its chief engraver, Christian Gobrecht.
lead
It was the last silver coin of that denomination to be struck before passage of the Coinage Act of 1873, which temporarily ended production of the silver dollar for American commerce.
lead
The coin's obverse is based on that of the Gobrecht dollar, which had been minted experimentally from 1836 to 1839.
lead

However, the soaring eagle used on the reverse of the Gobrecht dollar was not used; instead, the United States Mint (Mint) used a heraldic eagle, based on a design by late Mint Chief Engraver John Reich first utilized on coins in 1807.
lead
Seated Liberty dollars were initially struck only at the Philadelphia Mint; in 1846, production began at the New Orleans facility.
lead

In the late 1840s, the price of silver increased relative to gold because of an increase in supply of the latter caused by the California Gold Rush; this led to the hoarding, export, and melting of American silver coins.
lead

The Coinage Act of 1853 decreased the weight of all silver coins of five cents or higher, except for the dollar, but also required a supplemental payment from those wishing their bullion struck into dollar coins.
lead
As little silver was being presented to the US Mint at the time, production remained low.
Background
The Mint Act of 1792 made both gold and silver legal tender; specified weights of each was equal to a dollar.
Background
The United States Mint struck gold and silver only when depositors supplied metal, which was returned in the form of coin.
Background
In 1806, President Thomas Jefferson officially ordered all silver dollar mintage halted, though production had not occurred since 1804.
Background
In 1831, Mint Director Samuel Moore requested that President Andrew Jackson lift the restriction against dollar coin production; the president obliged in April of that year.
Background
Despite the approval to strike the coins, no silver dollars were minted until 1836.
Background
The Bureau of the Mint in the 1830s was undergoing a period of significant change, as new technologies were adopted.
Background
In 1828, the Mint, whose authorization had been subject to periodic renewal by Congress since its inception in 1792, was given permanent status.
Background
A new building to house the Philadelphia Mint was authorized by Congress, and opened in 1832.
Background

Congress adjusted the precious-metal content of US coins in 1834 and 1837, and was able to achieve a balance whereby US coins remained in circulation alongside those of foreign nations (mostly Spanish colonial pieces).
Background
In 1836, the first steam machinery was introduced at the Mint; previously coins had been struck by muscle power.
Background
Congress had in 1835 authorized branch mints at Dahlonega in Georgia, Charlotte in North Carolina, and at New Orleans in Louisiana.
Background

The Charlotte and Dahlonega mints only struck gold, catering to miners in the South who sought to deposit that metal, but the New Orleans facility would also strike silver coins, including the Seated Liberty dollar.
Gobrecht dollar

In an August 1, 1835, letter, Patterson proposed that Sully create an obverse design consisting of Liberty seated on a boulder, holding a " liberty pole " in her right hand topped by a pileus, the headgear given by the Romans to an emancipated slave.
Gobrecht dollar
Later in 1835, Christian Gobrecht was hired at the Mint as a draftsman, die sinker, and assistant engraver to Kneass.
Gobrecht dollar
Although nominally a subordinate, Gobrecht would perform much of the engraving work for the Mint until Kneass' death in 1840, when Gobrecht was appointed chief engraver.
Gobrecht dollar
Following a series of trial strikes and modifications through 1836, the first of what would come to be known as the Gobrecht dollars were minted in December of that year.
Gobrecht dollar
The dollars of 1836 were minted with a silver fineness of.892 (89.2%) silver, a specification set forth in the 1792 act.
Gobrecht dollar
The mandated fineness of US silver coins was changed from.892 to.900 (90%) by the Coinage Act of 1837, passed on January 18, 1837; subsequent Gobrecht dollars were struck in.900 silver.
Gobrecht dollar
Except on the half dime, abolished in 1873, the designs would remain on those coins for over 50 years.
Gobrecht dollar
Coinage continued in small amounts until 1839, when official production of the Gobrecht dollar ceased.
Gobrecht dollar
The Mint acquired a portrait lathe in 1837, which allowed Gobrecht to work in large models for the later versions of the Gobrecht dollar, and for the Seated Liberty dollar.
Gobrecht dollar
Prior to 1837, the engraver had to cut the design onto the die face by hand.
Design
Prior to full-scale production of a dollar coin in 1840, Patterson reviewed the designs then in use, including the Gobrecht dollar's.
Design

The director opted to replace Gobrecht's soaring eagle reverse with a left-facing bald eagle based on a design by former Mint engraver John Reich, a design first used on silver and gold coinage in 1807.
Design

Although the reverse for the dollar was probably selected to match that of the quarter and half dollar, it is not known why the flying eagle design was not used for the lower denominations in the first place.
Design

The neoclassical school was popular in the first half of the 19th century, and not only among official artists; Vermeule noted, "it becomes almost painfully evident that similar sources were consulted both by the engravers of United States coins in Philadelphia and by the cutters of tombstones from Maine to Illinois".
Design
Compared with the original Sully-Gobrecht conception of 1836–39, this is a sorry mess indeed."
Release
A small production run of 12,500 was minted in July 1840 to allow bullion depositors to become familiar with the new coins before having their silver struck into dollars.
Release
Bullion producers began depositing the silver required to initiate heavier production later in 1840; 41,000 pieces were minted in November, followed by a mintage of 7,505 in December.
Release
Deposits increased the following year, which saw a mintage of 173,000 pieces.
Release
All coins were produced at the Philadelphia Mint until 1846, when 59,000 were struck at the Mint at New Orleans.
Release
The influx caused the price of gold relative to silver to decrease, making silver coins worth more as bullion than as currency.
Release
As it was profitable to export silver, little was presented at the Mint, which resulted in low mintage numbers for the silver dollar; 1,300 and 1,100 were struck in 1851 and 1852 respectively.
Release
The rarity of these dates was recognized by the late 1850s; Mint employees made surreptitious restrikes to sell to collectors.
Release
Congress passed the Coinage Act of 1853 in February of that year.
Release
The act lowered the silver weight of the coins ranging from the half dime to half dollar by 6.9%, though the dollar remained unaffected.
Release
The 1853 act eliminated the practice of depositing silver bullion to be struck into coin, except into the dollar for which a coining charge of.5% was imposed.
Release
The silver dollar continued to circulate little; quantities were sent west beginning in 1854 to serve as "small change" in California.
Release
Silver prices remained high into the 1860s, and little silver bullion was presented for striking into dollars.
Release
To serve collectors, individual specimens were made available to the public by the Mint at a cost of $1.08.
Later years
David Bowers believes that most Seated Liberty dollars produced after 1853 were shipped to China to pay for luxury goods, including tea and silk.
Later years

However, although the Mint's Engraving Department sent dies for the dollar to the San Francisco facility repeatedly from 1858 on, the California mint used them only once before 1870, striking 20,000 dollars in 1859, a year in which 255,700 were struck at Philadelphia and 360,000 at New Orleans.
Later years
Production at New Orleans was disrupted after 1860 by the Civil War; it did not strike silver dollars again until 1879, after the end of the Seated Liberty series.
Later years
After the outbreak of the war in 1861, inflationary greenbacks were introduced, and precious-metal coins vanished from circulation.
Later years
In April 1863, new Mint Director James Pollock argued that the silver dollar be eliminated, noting in a letter that the coin "no longer enters into our monetary system.
Later years
In an October 21, 1863, report to Treasury Secretary Salmon P.
Later years

The Mint began producing patterns bearing various mottoes, including "God Our Trust" and "In God We Trust"; the latter was ultimately selected, and its first use was on the two-cent piece in 1864.The following year, a law was passed allowing the Treasury to place the motto upon any coin at its discretion.
Later years
The motto was placed on the silver dollar, as well as various other silver, gold and base metal coins, in 1866.
Later years
The Seated Liberty dollar was the first coin to be struck at the Carson City Mint; the first to be issued were 2,303 pieces paid to a Mr.
Later years
The dollar was struck at Carson City from 1870 to 1873, with the largest mintage, 11,758, in 1870.
Later years
The largest quantity struck at any mint was in 1872 at Philadelphia: 1,105,500, though the mintage in 1871 had also exceeded a million.
Abolition and aftermath
Beginning in 1859, large quantities of silver were found in Nevada Territory and elsewhere in the American West.
Abolition and aftermath
In 1869, Director of the Mint Henry Linderman began advocating the end of the acceptance of silver bullion deposits to be struck into dollars.
Abolition and aftermath

Although silver dollars were not coined in large numbers, Linderman saw that mining in the West would increase after the completion of the transcontinental railroad, which it did, as US silver production increased from 10 million troy ounces in 1867 to more than 22 million five years later.
Abolition and aftermath

Linderman foresaw that these activities would increase the supply of silver, causing its price to drop below the $1.2929 per ounce at which the precious metal in the standard silver dollar is worth $1.00.
Abolition and aftermath
The Coinage Act of 1873 ended production of the standard silver dollar and authorized creation of the Trade dollar, thus concluding the Seated Liberty dollar series.
Abolition and aftermath
Although not meant for use in the United States, a last-minute rider gave it legal tender status there up to $5.
Abolition and aftermath

When silver prices plummeted in the mid-1870s, millions appeared in circulation, at first in the West and then throughout the United States, causing problems in commerce when banks insisted on the $5 legal tender limit.
Abolition and aftermath
Other abuses followed, such as purchase by companies for bullion value (by then about $0.80) for use in pay packets.
Abolition and aftermath

In response to complaints, Congress ended any status as legal tender in 1876, halted production of the Trade dollar (except for collectors) in 1878, and agreed to redeem any which had not been chopmarked in 1887.
Abolition and aftermath

The 1873 act eliminated the provisions allowing depositors of silver bullion to have their metal struck into standard silver dollars; they could now only receive Trade dollars, which were not legal tender beyond $5.
Abolition and aftermath
As the price of silver then was about $1.30 per ounce, there was no outcry from silver producers.
Abolition and aftermath
Beginning in 1874, however, the price dropped; silver would not again sell for $1.2929 or more on the open market in the United States until 1963.
Abolition and aftermath

Many in Congress agreed, and the first battle over the issue resulted in a partial victory for silver forces, as the 1878 Bland–Allison Act required the Mint to purchase large quantities of silver on the open market and strike the bullion into dollar coins.
Abolition and aftermath
The issue of what monetary standard would be used occupied the nation for the rest of the 19th century, becoming most acute in the 1896 presidential election.
Abolition and aftermath
The issue was settled for the time by the Gold Standard Act of 1900, making that standard the law of the land.
Collecting

Considerable private melting in the early years of the series makes many dates rare; more melting took place when large quantities that had accumulated at the New York Sub-Treasury were sent to Philadelphia in 1861 and 1862 for restriking into smaller denominations.
Collecting
Yeoman 's 2014 edition of A Guide Book of United States Coins lists no Seated Liberty dollar in collectable condition (very good or better) at less than $280.
Collecting
The key dates of the series include the 1866 variety which lacks the motto "In God We Trust", of which only two are known; one sold at auction in 2005 for $1,207,500.
Collecting
Another rarity is the 1870 struck at San Francisco (1870-S), of which the mintage is not known as their striking was not recorded in that mint's records.
Collecting
There is no record of any 1870-dated obverse dies for the dollar being sent to San Francisco; nevertheless, the coins exist.
Collecting
Breen, writing in 1988, lists twelve examples known, which he speculates may have been presentation pieces, meant to be inserted in a cornerstone.
Collecting
One sold at auction for $1,092,500 in 2003.
Collecting
A similar mystery attends the 1873-S, which despite the stated mintage of 700, is not known to exist.
Collecting
Two of the pieces were routinely sent to Philadelphia for examination at the 1874 meeting of the United States Assay Commission, but apparently were not preserved.
Collecting
Breen suggests that the remaining mintage may have been melted along with obsolete silver coins.

lead

lead
Only 24 were minted, and of those, only nine are known to survive; all nine (as was the entire mintage) were proof coins; two are heavily worn impaired proofs.
lead
In 1957, one of the latter was found in a junk coin box at Gimbels Department Store, and purchased for $2.40.

In the first half of 1894, just 24 proofs of the Barber series dimes were manufactured at the San Francisco Mint.

Why only 24 of the coins were minted is unknown.

Three of the dimes were said to have been given to the superintendent's daughter, who allegedly spent one on a dish of ice cream and sold the other two in the 1950s.

Due to the rarity of the coin and the mysteries surrounding its past, the 1894-S dime is one of the most valuable coins produced in the United States.

1943 steel cents are U.S. one-cent coins that were struck in steel due to wartime shortages of copper.

The Philadelphia, Denver, and San Francisco mints each produced these 1943 Lincoln cents.
lead

After public outcry, the Mint developed a process whereby salvaged brass shell casings were augmented with pure copper to produce an alloy close to the 1941–42 composition.

This was used for 1944–46-dated cents, after which the prewar composition was resumed.

Although they continued to circulate into the 1960s, the mint collected large numbers of the 1943 cents and destroyed them.

(Even U.S. gold coins at various times contained from slightly over 2% copper to an eventual standard 10% copper to increase resistance to wear by making the pure gold coins slightly harder).

The error occurred when copper planchets were left in the press hopper and press machines during the changeover from copper to steel blanks.

cent_1793_chain_cent.title: Chain cent

Mint marks: None, all large cents were minted at the Philadelphia Mint

sents: lead
The chain cent was America 's first large cent and the first circulating coin officially produced by the United States Mint.
lead
It was not the first circulating coin produced by the United States, which was the Fugio cent of 1787 (also known as the Franklin cent), based on the Continental dollar.
lead
As with the Fugio cent, the Chain cent was made of copper and featured a chain symbolizing the linking together of the states of the United States.
Obverse design
The obverse design consisted of a stylized Liberty head with flowing hair, similar to that on the 1792 half disme but facing right.
Reverse design

The reverse 's central design figure, for which the coin is named, is an interlocking chain with 15 links, representing the fifteen American states in the Union at that time (the original Thirteen Colonies, Vermont and Kentucky).
Reverse design
Both the words "ONE CENT" and the fraction 1 / 100 appear within the chain.
Reverse design

sents: lead
The Lincoln cent (sometimes called the Lincoln penny) is a one-cent coin that has been struck by the United States Mint since 1909.
lead
The obverse or heads side was designed by Victor David Brenner, as was the original reverse, depicting two stalks of wheat (thus "wheat pennies", struck 1909–1958).
lead
The coin has seen several reverse, or tails, designs and now bears one by Lyndall Bass depicting a Union shield.
lead
All coins struck by the United States government with a value of 1 ⁄ 100 of a dollar are called cents because the United States has always minted coins using decimals.
lead
The penny nickname is a carryover from the coins struck in England, which went to decimals for coins in 1971.
lead
In 1905, sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens was hired by the Mint to redesign the cent and the four gold coins, which did not require congressional approval.
lead
Two of Saint-Gaudens's proposed designs for the cent were eventually adapted for the gold pieces, but Saint-Gaudens died in August 1907 before submitting additional designs for the cent.
lead
In January 1909, the Mint engaged Brenner to design a cent depicting the late president Abraham Lincoln, 1909 being the centennial year of his birth.
Inception
At Roosevelt's instructions, the Mint hired Saint-Gaudens to redesign the cent and the four gold pieces: the double eagle ($20), eagle ($10), half eagle ($5), and quarter eagle ($2.50).
Inception
As the designs of those pieces had remained the same for 25 years, they could be changed without an act of Congress.
Inception
The Indian Head cent, which the Lincoln cent replaced, had been introduced in 1859.
Inception
Saint-Gaudens originally conceived a flying eagle design for the cent, but at Roosevelt's request, developed it for the double eagle after learning that by law, an eagle could not appear on the cent.
Inception

Writer and friend Witter Bynner recalled that in January 1907, Saint-Gaudens was seriously ill with cancer, and was carried to his studio for ten minutes a day to critique the work of his assistants on current projects, including the cent.
Inception
Saint-Gaudens was by then in declining health; he died on August 3, 1907, without having submitted another design for the cent.
Inception
With the redesign of the four gold denominations completed by 1908, Roosevelt turned his attention to the cent.
Inception
The centennial of the birth of assassinated president Abraham Lincoln would occur in February 1909, and large numbers of privately manufactured souvenirs were already being issued.
Inception
Many writers had suggested a Lincoln half dollar, but that coin's design had been changed in 1892 and could not yet be altered without congressional approval.
Inception
In late 1908, Roosevelt sat for sculptor Victor David Brenner, who was designing a medal for the Panama Canal Commission.
Inception
While the contents of their conversations were never recorded, it appears they discussed Roosevelt's plans for coinage redesign.
Inception
Roosevelt had admired a 1907 plaque of Lincoln which the artist had produced.
Design
Brenner's obverse design closely follows a profile of Lincoln he had used in other work, such as the desk plaque he made for the Gorham Manufacturing Company in 1907.
Design
Numismatic historian Roger Burdette suggests that Brenner based his work on an 1864 photograph of Lincoln taken at Mathew Brady 's studio by one of his assistants.
Design
As the photograph in question only showed Lincoln's head and shoulders, Reed indicates that Brenner obtained additional detail from an 1860 campaign photograph of a beardless Lincoln.
Design

On January 18, 1909, Brenner submitted models to the Mint with a Lincoln profile on the obverse, and a reverse design very similar to that on the then-current French silver coins, showing a tree branch.
Design
Leach replied on February 2 that no change to the half dollar could be made without congressional approval.
Design

Brenner worked quickly, and on February 17, delivered models for both obverse and reverse similar to the eventual coin, though with a somewhat larger bust of Lincoln, and the motto " In God We Trust " omitted.
Design
On March 4, 1909, the day on which Roosevelt left office, replaced by William Howard Taft, Brenner met with Mint Engraver Charles E.
Design
On March 15, Brenner wrote to Leach stating that Barber seemed in no hurry to have the new coins produced.
Design
I have to inform you that I was not satisfied with the first proof of the Lincoln cent.
Design
On May 26, samples of the new coin with and without the motto were shown to President Taft, who selected the mottoed version.
Design
The coin was formally approved by Secretary of the Treasury Franklin MacVeagh on July 14 and a release date of August 2, 1909, was set.
Release
The Philadelphia Mint struck 20,000,000 of the new coin even before its design was made official by Secretary MacVeagh.
Release
Dies for the San Francisco Mint, prepared at Philadelphia, were ready for shipment to San Francisco on June 22.
Release
The Mint decided to plan for a simultaneous release of the coin across the United States on August 2, and Treasury Department branches were sent what were thought to be adequate supplies.
Release
On the morning of August 2, 1909, long lines formed outside Treasury facilities across the United States.
Release

Some early applicants were able to obtain all the coins they wanted, but soon the pieces were rationed: applicants at the New York Sub-Treasury were allowed 100 pieces per person; those who sought the coins at the Philadelphia Mint were allowed only two each.
Brenner's initials

Brenner's initials, which he had placed at the base of the reverse, immediately became a source of controversy—on the afternoon of August 2, The Washington Star queried the Treasury as to the initials.
Brenner's initials
On August 5, Secretary MacVeagh ordered coinage of the cent suspended until the coins could be struck with an inconspicuous "B" for Brenner on the coin.
Brenner's initials

Treasury Department Solicitor Maurice O'Connell held that the exclusion of the initials did not constitute a design change which could only have been implemented by waiting 25 years or obtaining congressional approval.
Brenner's initials
The cents without Brenner's initials were in production by August 12, 1909.
Brenner's initials
Barber was recalled from his vacation in Cape May, New Jersey, to deal with the complaints.
Brenner's initials
By the end of 1909, supply of the new cents was finally up to demand.
Production
Cents with and without Brenner's initials were struck at both Philadelphia and San Francisco in 1909.
Production

While almost 28 million Philadelphia VDB cents were struck, making them quite common, the 1909-S with Brenner's initials (commonly called the 1909-S VDB) is the rarest Lincoln cent by date and mintmark, with only 484,000 released for circulation.
Production
In 1911, the Denver Mint began striking cents with the mintmark D, and in most years in the following decades, all three mints struck cents.
Production
In 1916, Barber modified the design, causing Lincoln's cheek and coat to appear less wrinkled.
Production
In 1917, a year which saw Barber's death in office at age 77, the wartime economy caused a shortage of cents.
Production
In 1918, Brenner's initials were restored to the coin, appearing where Lincoln's shoulder is cut off by the rim of the coin.
Production
The recession year of 1922 saw a lower-than-usual demand for coins in commerce, and few cents were coined.
Production
At the time, dies were only made at Philadelphia; the Denver Mint had outstanding orders for cents that year.
Production
On many strikes, the mintmark on the die filled with oil and dirt, producing coins on which the mintmark does not appear, or appears only faintly.
Production
The 1922 plain piece is another relatively rare one in the Lincoln cent series.
Production
When the 25-year period during which the Lincoln cent could not be changed without congressional approval expired, there was no interest in replacing the design as the coin had remained popular.
Production
Beginning in 1936, proof coins were struck for collectors for the first time since 1916.

Made only at Philadelphia, these pieces were coined from dies polished to mirror smoothness.

With the US entry into World War II in 1941, copper and tin, which were both used in the cent, were in short supply.

Low-grade carbon steel formed the base of these coins, to which a zinc coating 0.0005-inch (0.013 mm) thick was deposited on each side electrolytically as a rust preventive.

lead

lead

lead

lead

This statute gave the United States authority to sell metal to the British government from up to 350,000,000 silver dollars at $1 per ounce of silver plus the value of the copper in the coins, and handling and transportation fees.

Circulating Eisenhower dollars contained no silver, though some for collectors were struck in 40% silver.

The US Mint released order information in the spring, with the coins priced at $85.

Reverse proof, as part of a 2-coin set including a Morgan Dollar, minted by the San Francisco Mint, S mint mark, 250,000 mintage limit.
Modern Peace Dollars
The Uncirculated 2023 Peace Dollar was released on July 13, 2023, and sold out on the first day.
Modern Peace Dollars
The Proof 2023 Peace Dollar was released on August 9, 2023.

Gold: 2014 commemorative version: 0.999 fine gold, 0.75 troy oz
Silver: Silver collectors' versions: 1976: 40% fine, 0.37 troy oz. Silver proofs 1992–2018: 90% fine, 0.402 troy oz. Silver proofs since 2019: 99.9% fine, 0.37 troy oz

Mint mark located beneath where the eagle's claws grasp the olive branch on reverse for 1964 coins and for 1964-2014-W gold issue; above the date on the obverse for all other issues. sents: lead
The Kennedy half dollar, first minted in 1964, is a fifty-cent coin issued by the United States Mint.
lead
Intended as a memorial to the assassinated 35th president of the United States John F.
lead
Kennedy, it was authorized by Congress just over a month after his death.
lead
Use of existing works by Mint sculptors Gilroy Roberts and Frank Gasparro allowed dies to be prepared quickly, and striking of the new coins began in January 1964.
lead
The silver coins were hoarded upon their release in March 1964 by collectors and those interested in a memento of the late president.
lead
Although the Mint greatly increased production, the denomination was seldom seen in circulation.
lead
Continued rises in the price of silver increased the hoarding—many early Kennedy half dollars have been melted for their silver content.
lead
Starting with 1965-dated coins, the percentage of fine silver was reduced from 90% to 40% (silver clad), but even with this change the coin saw little circulation.
Inception

Kennedy on November 22, 1963, Mint Director Eva Adams called Chief Engraver Gilroy Roberts, informing him that serious consideration was already being given to depicting Kennedy on one of the larger silver coins: either the silver dollar, half dollar, or quarter dollar.
Inception

In 1962, President Kennedy had three hundred appreciation medals struck by the United States Mint in Philadelphia that were later presented during his June 23, 1963 through July 2, 1963 trip to the nations of Federal Republic of Germany, Germany (West Berlin), Ireland, United Kingdom, Italy, and the Vatican City State.
Inception
Congressional approval was required for any design change within 25 years of the last.
Inception

On December 10, the new President, Lyndon Johnson, endorsed the call for a Kennedy half dollar, asking Congress to pass the legislation promptly to allow striking of the new piece to begin early in 1964.
Inception
The bill to authorize the Kennedy half dollar passed on December 30, 1963.
Inception
Work was already underway on coinage dies; the use of the already-available designs allowed for the completion of the first dies on January 2, 1964.
Inception
Only proof coins were initially struck.
Inception
The first Kennedy half dollars intended for circulation were struck at the Denver Mint on January 30, 1964, followed by the Philadelphia Mint the next week.
Inception
A ceremonial first strike was held at both Philadelphia and Denver on February 11, 1964.
Initial popularity
The Treasury Department made the coins available to the public beginning on March 24, 1964.
Initial popularity
A line a block long formed at the department's windows in Washington to purchase the 70,000 coins initially allocated for public sale.
Initial popularity
Although the department limited sales to 40 per customer, by the end of the day, the coins were gone, but the line had not shortened.
Initial popularity

Sales in New York did not begin until the following day, and rationing was imposed there as well, to the disgruntlement of the head of the coin department at Gimbels, the largest dealer in the city, which had hoped to sell the coins at a premium.
Initial popularity
The Treasury had initially planned to issue 91 million half dollars for 1964, but raised the number to 141 million.
Initial popularity
By late November, the Mint had struck approximately 160 million pieces, yet the coin was almost never seen in circulation.
Initial popularity
Hopeful that issuing more 1964-dated coins would counter the speculation in them, the Treasury requested and received Congressional authorization to continue striking 1964-dated coins into 1965.
Initial popularity
Eventually, almost 430 million half dollars dated 1964 were struck, a sum greater than the total struck for circulation in the sixteen years of the Franklin half dollar series.
Initial popularity
Prices for the metal were rising to such an extent that, by early June, a dime contained 9.33 cents' worth of silver at market prices.
Initial popularity
On June 3, 1965, President Johnson announced plans to eliminate silver from the dime and quarter in favor of a clad sandwich with layers of copper-nickel on each side of a layer of pure copper.
Initial popularity
The half dollar was changed from 90% silver to 40%.
Initial popularity
The new half dollars retained their silvery appearance, due to the outer layer being 80% silver and 20% copper.
Initial popularity
The coin was also minted with an inner layer of 21% silver and 79% copper.
Initial popularity
The first silver-clad half dollars were struck at the Denver Mint on December 30, 1965, bearing the date 1965; the date would not be changed for all US coinage until the coin shortage was eased.
Initial popularity
Beginning on August 1, 1966, the Mint began to strike 1966-dated pieces, and thereafter it resumed the normal practice of striking the current year's date on each piece.
Initial popularity
In the meantime, Washington quarters, the same design used since 1932, became the highest value coin of the realm, in terms of circulation use.
Initial popularity
Today, this continues to be the case, and Kennedy half dollars as well as the later mini-dollar coins, are almost never encountered."

In May 1969, the Treasury sought authorization to eliminate the half dollar's silver content, changing it to the same copper-nickel clad composition as the dime and quarter.
Switch to base metal

The dispute dragged on for over a year before President Nixon signed a bill on December 31, 1970 which authorized production of the Eisenhower dollar and eliminated the remaining 40% silver content from the half dollar.
Switch to base metal
As a result of the delay, in 1970 uncirculated (non-proof) half dollars were struck only at the Denver mint and were available solely in mint sets.
Switch to base metal

Switch to base metal

Switch to base metal

Switch to base metal
The Mint had anticipated a dramatic comeback for the denomination, but only a moderate increase in the usage of half dollars was noted after the 1971 clad coins were issued.
Switch to base metal

On October 18, President Nixon signed Public Law 93-127, which provided for new reverse designs for the quarter, half dollar, and dollar.

All half dollars struck in 1975 and 1976 bore the double date 1776–1976 on the obverse and Huntington's design on the reverse.

Over 521 million Bicentennial half dollars were struck for circulation.

They do go somewhere, though, so someone must want them." By then, more than 2.5 billion Kennedy half dollars had been struck since 1964, more than all previously struck US half dollars combined.

The silver boom of 1979–80 saw a large increase in the amount of sales and destruction of many hoarded 1964–1969 silver Kennedy half dollars.

Kennedy half dollars began to be produced for general circulation again in 2021.

With the exception of 1965 through 1967, proofs have been struck each year in the same metallic composition as regular issue pieces.

The first Kennedy half dollar proofs were struck in early January 1964.

Early strikes depicted Kennedy with heavily accented hair; an estimated 100,000 coins were struck with this feature.
Collecting
Due to the coin shortage, the Treasury Department announced that no proof sets would be struck in 1965.
Collecting
Coins for these sets, minted at the San Francisco Assay Office, were struck with no mint marks early in 1966 with heavily polished dies dated 1965.
Collecting
Similar sets bearing the dates 1966 and 1967 were also struck.
Collecting
A few of the 1966 halves from the Special Mint Sets are known with Gasparro's initials " FG " missing from the reverse, apparently because of an overpolished die.
Collecting
The first year's production was sold in soft plastic packaging; the 1966 and 1967 issues were sonically sealed in hard plastic cases.
Collecting
In 1968, regular proof coinage was resumed, although production of proof coins was shifted to San Francisco, the "S" mintmark added and sets were encapsulated in hard plastic.
Collecting
In 1973, Congress authorized silver-clad collector versions of the Bicentennial coins; in April 1975, the Mint began to strike them.
Collecting
Copper-nickel clad Bicentennial coins were placed in both the 1975 and 1976 proof sets, while their silver clad counterparts were sold in three-coin sets.
Collecting
Since 1992, the Mint has struck Kennedy half dollars in 90% silver for inclusion in special silver proof sets.
Collecting
1964 proofs were struck in Philadelphia, and since 1968, proof coins have been struck in San Francisco only.
Collecting
In 1998, some silver proof pieces were struck to a matte finish for inclusion in a set along with a Robert F.
Collecting
From 2005–2010, uncirculated pieces included in mint sets received a matte finish, which differentiates them from the pieces sold in bags and rolls.
Collecting
It is the rarest non-error variety of the Kennedy half known to date.
Collecting
Examples of this variety typically sell for significant amounts of money; a 1964 Special Mint Set half dollar sold for $47,000 in 2016.
Collecting
In 1998, a special "matte finish" Kennedy half dollar was issued as part of the two-coin "Kennedy Collectors Set", paired with a commemorative silver dollar honoring Robert F.
Collecting
Between 62,000 and 64,000 1998-S, matte finish coins were issued, making it the lowest mintage of the series.
Collecting

Half dollars not intended for circulation, such as proof coins and those minted with dates 2002 through 2020 occasionally enter circulation; these issues are sometimes found through coin roll hunting by collectors, being referred to as 'NIFCs' (Not Intended For Circulation).
Collecting
In 2019, an Enhanced Reverse Proof Kennedy half dollar was included in a special set with an Apollo 11 50th anniversary half dollar.
Collecting
The special Kennedy half was limited to a maximum mintage of 100,000 coins and sold out.

The Denver Mint, established in 1906, struck the coins for only one year, in 1921.

The act was repealed on November 1, 1893.

On June 13, 1898, Congress ordered the coining of all the remaining bullion purchased under the Sherman Silver Purchase Act into silver dollars.

The U.S. eventually melted a total of 270,232,722 silver dollars.

Of that amount, 259,121,554 were sold to the United Kingdom at the cost of one dollar per troy ounce.

During the same year, the Peace dollar was first issued to commemorate the end of World War I.

Treasury discovered previously unknown mint bags in its vaults containing slightly more than 2.8 million Carson City silver dollars.

San Francisco commemorative dollar reverse
In total, 100,000 gold and 500,000 silver commemorative coins were authorized.

Mint artist Joseph Menna made a new model for the reverse, employing a 1904 San Francisco-minted dollar as his model.

House of Representatives passed legislation to allow the minting of Morgan and Peace dollar coins in 2021, the 100-year anniversary of the transition from the Morgan to Peace dollar in order to "commemorate this significant evolution of American Freedom".
Modern Morgan Dollars
On December 18, 2020, the United States Senate unanimously approved the bill, and it was signed into law by President Donald Trump on January 5, 2021.
Modern Morgan Dollars

The Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee unanimously approved the design on January 19, 2021, with recommendations which were sent to the Secretary of the Treasury Steven Mnuchin, one day before the end of the Trump administration.

There is no known mintage limit, and mintage could not begin until after January 1, 2021.

The US Mint then released order information for both dollars, priced at $85 apiece.

Both coins are "0.858 troy oz. of.999 fine silver with an uncirculated finish" Morgan Dollars were made available for purchase in May 2021, and sold out on the U.S.

Mint website in 45 minutes, and had a staggered order window based on the different mint marks.
Modern Morgan Dollars
Mint ordering procedures and resulted in delays from the originally intended release dates.
Modern Morgan Dollars
The 2021 Morgan Dollars were minted in the active mints of Philadelphia (no mint mark), Denver (D), and San Francisco (S).
Modern Morgan Dollars
The 2021 Peace Dollars had no mint mark and were only minted in Philadelphia.
Modern Morgan Dollars
After the chaos caused by the CC and O dollars, the Household Order Limit was reduced from 10 to 3 for the remainder of the dollars.
Modern Morgan Dollars
The 2023 Uncirculated Morgan Dollar was released by the US Mint on July 13, 2023, and sold out on the first day of issue.
Mintage figures
The dollars were produced every year between 1878 and 1904 at a total of four different mints.
Mintage figures
In 1921 production was resumed for one year only, with this year being the only one where the Denver mint was used, until 2021.
Mintage figures
The number of dollars surviving are unknown as the Pittman Act resulted in the melting of millions of these coins, and the individual dates melted were never recorded.
Mintage figures
PCGS CoinFacts estimates survivals are less than 10% of the mintage.
Mintage figures
Note that of the 2021 Philadelphia Morgan Dollars, a third were minted with a "CC" privy mark and a third were minted with an "O" privy mark.

lead
The largest denomination of United States coin authorized by the Mint Act of 1792 was the eagle, or ten-dollar piece.

The large amount of bullion being brought east after the discovery of gold in California in the 1840s caused Congress to consider new denominations of gold coinage.

The double eagle soon became the most popular gold coin in terms of the number of pieces struck.
During the denomination's life, from 1850 to 1933, far more gold was struck into double eagles than into all other denominations combined.

Of all gold coins struck from the start of gold coinage for circulation in 1795 to the end in 1933, just under half of the coins struck were double eagles, but 78% of the gold used was struck into twenty-dollar pieces.
According to Bowers, the double eagle "represented the most efficient way to coin a given quantity of gold bullion into coin form".
Regular production of the double eagle began with the striking of just over a million at Philadelphia in 1850, and 141,000 at the New Orleans Mint that year.
