wrld_1741_austria_maria_theresa_tha.title: Maria Theresa thaler
sents: lead
The Maria Theresa thaler (MTT) is a silver bullion coin and a type of Conventionsthaler that has been used in world trade continuously since it was first minted in 1741.
lead
It is named after Maria Theresa who ruled Austria, Hungary, and Bohemia from 1740 to 1780 and is depicted on the coin.
History
In 1741, the first MTT was struck according to the Reichsthaler standard with 1 ⁄ 9 of a Cologne mark of fine silver, or 25.98 grams.
History
In 1750 a new thaler was struck with a gross weight of 1 ⁄ 10 of 1 Vienna mark of silver, 5 ⁄ 6 fine (with a fine silver content of 23.39 grams, or 1 ⁄ 10 of a Cologne mark).
History
In 1751 this new standard Conventionsthaler was effectively adopted across the German-speaking world when it was accepted formally in the Bavarian monetary convention.
History
Since the death of Maria Theresa in 1780, the coin has always been dated 1780.
History
On 19 September 1857, Emperor Francis Joseph of Austria declared the Maria Theresa thaler to be an official trade coinage.
History
A little over a year later, on 31 October 1858, it lost its status as a currency in Austria.
History

During the Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies in World War II, enough people preferred it to the money issued by the occupying forces that the American Office of Strategic Services created counterfeit MTTs for use by resistance forces.
History
In German-speaking countries, following a spelling reform dated 1901 that took effect two years later, Thaler is written Taler (the spelling of given names like Theresa was not affected).
History
Hence 20th-century references to this coin in German and Austrian sources are found under Maria-Theresien-Taler.
Details
The thaler is 39.5–41 mm (1.56–1.61 in) in diameter and 2.5 mm (0.098 in) thick, weighs 28.0668 grams (0.99003 oz) and contains 23.386 grams (0.752 troy ounces) of fine silver.
Details
It has a silver content of.833 and a copper content of.166 of its total millesimal fineness.
Details
Note: Rome mint struck MTTs are marginally lighter being produced in finer 835-standard instead of 833-standard silver.
Details
1780 ☓, which means, 'Maria Theresa, by the grace of God, Empress of the Romans, Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, Archduchess of Austria, Duchess of Burgundy, Countess of Tyrol.
Details
The "☓" is a saltire or Burgundian cross, and was added in 1750 indicating the new debased standard of the thaler.
Minting outside of Austria
Between 1751 and 2000, some 389 million were minted.
Minting outside of Austria
In 1935 Mussolini gained a 25-year concession over the production of the MTT.
Minting outside of Austria
In 1961 the 25-year concession ended and Austria made diplomatic approaches to the relevant governments requesting they cease production of the coin.
Minting outside of Austria
The UK was the last government to agree formally to the request in February 1962.
Minting outside of Austria
The Italian government produced a similarly designed coin in the hope of replacing the Maria Theresa thaler, but it never gained acceptance.
Minting outside of Austria
In the United Kingdom, the Maria Theresa thaler bearing the date of 1780 is a "protected coin" for of Part II of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981.
Ethiopia
The MTT is first recorded as circulating in Ethiopia from Emperor Iyasu II of Ethiopia (1730–1755).
Ethiopia
According to traveller James Bruce, the coin, not debased as other currencies, dominated the areas he visited in 1768.
Ethiopia
Joseph Kalmer and Ludwig Hyun in the book Abessinien estimate that over 20% of 245 million coins minted until 1931 ended up in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia
In 1868, the British military expedition to Magdala, the capital of Emperor Tewodros II of Ethiopia, under Field Marshal Robert Napier, took MTTs with them to pay local expenses.
Ethiopia
In 1890 the Italians introduced the Tallero Eritreo, styled after the MTT, in their new colony Eritrea, also hoping to impose it on the commerce with Ethiopia.
Ethiopia
In the early 1900s, Menelik II unsuccessfully attempted to mint Menelik thalers locally, with his effigy, but styled following the model of the MTT, and force their use.
Ethiopia
Starting in 1935 the Italians minted the MTT at the mint in Rome for use in their conquest of Ethiopia.
Ethiopia
Then during World War II, the British minted some 18 million MTTs in Bombay to use in their East African Campaign to drive the Italians out of Ethiopia.

wrld_1966_mexico_hidalgo_10_pesos.title: Mexican peso
sents: lead

The Mexican peso (symbol: $; currency code: MXN; also abbreviated Mex$ to distinguish it from other peso-denominated currencies; referred to as the peso, Mexican peso, or colloquially varo) is the official currency of Mexico.
lead
The peso was first introduced in 1863, replacing the old Spanish colonial real.
lead
The Mexican peso is subdivided into 100 centavos, represented by " ¢ ".
lead
Mexican banknotes are issued by the Bank of Mexico in various denominations and feature vibrant colors and imagery representing Mexican culture and history.
lead
Modern peso and dollar currencies have a common origin in the 16th–19th century Spanish dollar, most continuing to use its sign, "$".
lead
The current ISO 4217 code for the peso is MXN; the "N" refers to the "new peso".
lead
Prior to the 1993 revaluation, the code MXP was used.
lead

The Mexican peso is the 16th most traded currency in the world, the third most traded currency from the Americas (after the United States dollar and Canadian dollar), and the most traded currency from Latin America.
Precursor
15 or 16 silver reales were worth a gold escudo, and eight-real coins of 24.44 g fine silver were widely called pesos in Spanish America and dollars in Britain and its American colonies.
Precursor
Mexican silver pesos of original cap-and-ray design were legal tender in the United States until 1857 and in China until 1935.
Origin
The post-independence silver peso contained 27.07 grams of 90.3% fine silver (24.44 g fine) while the gold peso or half escudo contained 1.6915 grams of 87.5% fine gold (1.48 g fine).
Origin

After most of Europe switched to the gold standard in the 1870s the gold peso substantially rose in value against the silver peso, until it became 2 silver pesos to a gold peso or a gold peso dollar by 1900.
Origin
From 1918 onward the weight and fineness of all the silver coins declined, until 1979, when the last silver 100-peso coins were minted.
Origin
The U.S. dollar was worth 2.00 silver pesos from 1905 to 1929, rising afterward until it stabilized at 12.50 pesos from 1954 to 1976.
Reformation

Throughout most of the 20th century, the Mexican peso remained one of the more stable currencies in Latin America, since the economy did not experience periods of hyperinflation common to other countries in the region.
Devaluations in 1976 and 1982
The U.S. dollar leapt from 12.50 to 19.40 pesos in 1976.
Devaluations in 1976 and 1982
After the oil crisis of the late 1970s, Mexico defaulted on its external debt in 1982, causing severe capital flight and several years of inflation and devaluation.
New peso, 1993
On January 1, 1993, the Bank of Mexico introduced a new currency, the nuevo peso ("new peso", or MXN), written "N$" followed by the numerical amount.
New peso, 1993
One new peso, or N$1.00, was equal to 1,000 of the obsolete MXP pesos.
New peso notes and coins
For example, the Series A old peso MXP$20,000 and the Series B nuevo peso MXN$20 banknotes share the same design, aside from the updated face value.
New peso notes and coins

Old and new pesos circulated simultaneously between 1993 and 1995, but old peso Series A banknotes were gradually retired at this time, and newly designed Series C "nuevo peso" banknotes commenced in 1994.
New peso notes and coins
From January 1, 1996, the "nuevo peso" was simply renamed to "peso", and new Series D banknotes were issued identical to Series C except for the word "nuevo" dropped.
New peso notes and coins
Series A and AA banknotes were demonetized and no longer legal tender as of January 1, 1996.
New peso notes and coins
Although they remain legal tender, Series B, C, D, and D1 banknotes are in the process of being withdrawn from circulation; in addition, the MXN$1000 Series F banknote is being withdrawn.
New peso notes and coins
The most commonly circulated banknotes in Mexico are MXN$20 and above in Series F and G.
New peso notes and coins
Similarly, Series B coins in nuevo peso denominations were circulated starting from 1993 and Series A and AA coins were demonetized starting from November 15, 1995.
New peso notes and coins
Series C coins (which dropped the "N$" prefix on the MXN$1, N$5, N$10, N$20, and N$50 coins) were circulated starting in 1996 following the withdrawal of Series A and AA coins.
New peso notes and coins
Series B and C coins in uncommon denominations (10-centavo and MXN$20 and greater) are gradually being withdrawn from circulation.
New peso notes and coins
The most commonly circulated coins in Mexico are MXN$10 and below in Series C and D.
Economic effects
The government's operational balances had been predicted to remain stable as the country was operating in a surplus between 1990 and 1994.
Economic effects

The volatility of MXN increased after the ratification of NAFTA, when the annualized standard deviations seem to be highest post-1994, especially in terms of USD, compared to the United States, which experienced the lowest annualized standard deviation during that same period.
Economic effects
The adoption of MXN in 1993 was meant to balance the economy, and MXP 1000 was the same as MXN 1 upon its 1993 introduction.
Economic effects

As the GNP fell by 9.2% in 1995, the panic of the MXN devaluation was significant to Mexican citizens, as the peso depreciated against the USD by 82.9%, while the interest rates rose from 10.5 to 42.7%.
Economic effects
Married women with an unemployed husband experienced an employment rate of 33.84% and an unemployment rate of 1.62% compared with unmarried women during this period.
Subsequent exchange rates
Following the revaluation in 1993, the official exchange rate was MXN$3 against the U.S. dollar.
Subsequent exchange rates
After the Mexican peso crisis of December 1994, the peso sharply depreciated from MXN$3.4 to MXN$7.2 in 1995.
Subsequent exchange rates

It then traded between MXN$8 and MXN$11 from 1998 to 2008, briefly depreciated to MXN$15.56 in March 2009 due to the 2008 global financial crisis, but then settled between MXN$12 and MXN$14 from 2009 to 2014.
Subsequent exchange rates
The peso then depreciated from MXN$14.78 in 2014 to MXN$17 in 2015.
Subsequent exchange rates
From 2016 to 2019, it traded between MXN$18 and MXN$20.
Subsequent exchange rates
Amidst the COVID-19 pandemic, the peso depreciated to its all-time low of MXN$25 per dollar.
Subsequent exchange rates
From 2020 to 2024, it appreciated by over 30%, becoming one of the best performing currencies in the world.
Subsequent exchange rates
In April 2024, the peso reached a near nine-year high of MXN$16.26 per dollar.
Subsequent exchange rates
Since the general elections in 2024, the peso has depreciated to over MXN$20.
Real
in gold: 1 ⁄ 2, 1, 2, 4 and 8 escudos, with 1 escudo ≈ 2 pesos or 16 reales.
Peso, 19th century

The Second Mexican Empire of 1863-1867 commenced the minting of coins denominated in pesos and centavos, minting the copper 1-centavo, silver 5, 10 and 50 centavos, the silver 1-peso and the gold 20-peso.
Peso, 19th century
The copper 1-centavo coin was continued; silver (.9027 fine) coins of 5, 10, 20, 25 and 50 centavos and 1 peso commenced in 1867; and gold coins of 1, 2 + 1 ⁄ 2, 5, 10 and 20 pesos commenced in 1870.
Peso, 19th century
In 1882, cupro-nickel 1, 2 and 5 centavos coins were issued but they were only minted for two years.
Peso, 20th century
In 1905 a monetary reform was carried out in which the gold content of the peso was reduced by 49.36% and the silver coins were (with the exception of the 1-peso) reduced to token issues.
Peso, 20th century
Bronze 1 and 2 centavos, nickel 5 centavos, silver 10, 20, and 50 centavos and gold 5 and 10 pesos were issued.
Peso, 20th century
In 1910, a new peso coin was issued, the famous Caballito, considered one of the most beautiful of Mexican coins.
Peso, 20th century
In 1947, a new issue of silver coins was struck, with the 50 centavo and 1 peso in.500 fineness and a new 5-peso coin in.900 fineness.
Peso, 20th century
A portrait of José María Morelos appeared on the 1 peso, with Cuauhtémoc appearing on the 5-peso; and this was to remain a feature of the 1 peso coin until its demise.
Peso, 20th century
A new portrait of Morelos appeared on the 1 peso, with Cuauhtemoc now on the 50 centavo and Miguel Hidalgo on the 5 peso coins.
Peso, 20th century
During this period 5 peso, and to a lesser extent, 10 peso coins were also used as vehicles for occasional commemorative strikings.
Peso, 20th century
Between 1960 and 1971, new coinage was introduced, consisting of brass 1 and 5 centavos, cupro-nickel 10, 25, and 50 centavos, 1, 5, and 10 pesos, and silver 25 pesos (only issued 1968 and 1972).
Peso, 20th century
In 1980, smaller 5 peso coins were introduced alongside 20 pesos and (from 1982) 50-pesos in cupro-nickel.
Peso, 20th century
Between 1978 and 1982, the sizes of the coins for 20 centavos and above were reduced.
Peso, 20th century
Base metal 100, 200, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 peso coins were introduced between 1984 and 1988.
New peso coins
In 1993, President Carlos Salinas de Gortari stripped three zeros from the peso, creating a parity of 1 new peso for 1,000 of the old ones.
New peso coins
Bimetallic 10, 20 and 50 nuevos pesos, with sterling silver (0.925 fine) centers and aluminum bronze rings.
New peso coins

Though the 50- and 100-peso coins are the only currently circulating coinage in the world to contain any silver, they rarely circulate because their silver content of 1/2 troy ounce have exceeded 100 pesos in value since around 2010.
New peso coins
In 2003 the Banco de México began the gradual launch of a new series of bimetallic $100 coins.
New peso coins
In circulation, they are extraordinarily rare, but their novelty value offsets the unease most users feel at having such a large amount of money in a single coin.
New peso coins
The first C1-type coins were issued in 2020; in general, these are commemorative $20 coins.
New peso coins
As of 2020, the coins most commonly encountered in circulation have face values of 50¢, $1, $2, $5 and $10.
New peso coins
Commemorative $20 coins are less commonly encountered than $20 notes.
New peso coins
The 5¢ coin has been withdrawn from circulation in 2002, while the 10¢ and 20¢ coins have gradually dropped out of circulation due to their low value.
First
The first banknotes issued by the Mexican state were produced in 1823 by Emperor Agustin de Iturbide in denominations of 1, 2 and 10 pesos.
First
In 1920, the Monetary Commission (Comisión Monetaria) issued 50-centavos and 1-peso notes whilst the Bank of Mexico (Banco de México) issued 2-pesos notes.
First
From 1925, the Bank issued notes for 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 pesos, with 500 and 1000 pesos following in 1931.
First
From 1935, the Bank also began issuing a new series of banknotes (Series AA) including 1-peso notes and, from 1945, 10,000 pesos.
First
The banknote of 10,000 pesos was kept in circulation between 1945 and 1956 and was put into circulation again in 1979, being replaced by the 10,000 banknotes that would come into circulation in 1982.
First
Production of 1-peso notes ceased in 1970, followed by 5 pesos in 1972, 10 and 20 pesos in 1977, 50 pesos in 1984, 100 pesos in 1985, 500 pesos in 1987 and 1,000 pesos in 1988.
First

A new series (Series A) were issued starting from 1980: 5,000-pesos notes were introduced in 1980, followed by 2,000 pesos in 1983, 20,000 pesos in 1985, 50,000 pesos in 1986 and 100,000 pesos in 1991.
Series B
In 1993, notes were introduced in the new currency for 10, 20, 50, and 100 nuevos pesos.
Series B
(This series designation is not the 1 or 2 letter series label printed on the banknotes themselves.) All were printed with the date July 31, 1992.
Series C

The ducat (/ ˈ d ʌ k ə t /) coin was used as a trade coin in Europe from the later Middle Ages to the 19th century.

Similarly named silver ducatons also existed.
lead
The gold ducat circulated along with the Florentine florin and preceded both the modern British pound sterling and the United States dollar.

The first issue of scyphate billon coins modelled on Byzantine trachea was made by King Roger II of Sicily as part of the Assizes of Ariano (1140).
Predecessors

The first issue bears the figure of Christ and the Latin inscription Sit tibi, Christe, datus, quem tu regis iste ducatus (meaning "O Christ, let this duchy, which you rule, be dedicated to you") on the obverse.

In the 13th century, the Venetians imported goods from the East and sold them at a profit north of the Alps.

In 1252 Florence and Genoa introduced the gold florin and genovino, respectively, both of 3.5 grams of 98.6% fine gold; the florin preceded the ducat as Western Europe's first standard gold coin.

Continued depreciation in the silver currency during the 16th century, however, made the gold ducat worth more than 124 soldi.

Leonardo Loredan extended the coinage with a half ducat and subsequent doges added a quarter, and various multiples up to 105 ducats.

Subsequent grand masters, however, found it expedient to copy the Venetian types more exactly, first at Rhodes and then on Malta.

Genoese traders went further; they struck ducats at Chios that could be distinguished from the Venetian originals only by their workmanship.

The rarity of ducats that Genoese traders struck at Mytilene, Phocaea, and Pera suggests that Venetians melted those they encountered.

In Western Europe, Venice was an active trader but they sold more than they bought, thus giving the Florentine florin an early foothold in the Rhine river valley in 1354.

23¾ carats fine and slightly smaller than the Venetian ducat, each had about 3.484 g of pure gold and was reckoned as 375 maravedís, the typical unit of account at the time.

Background and authorisation
It had a diameter of 42 millimetres (1.7 in), and weighed 15.55 grams (0.500 troy ounces), twice the weight of the existing gold coin, the ryal.
Background and authorisation
The new coin was struck in response to a large influx of gold into Europe from West Africa in the 1480s, and Henry at first called it the double ryal, but soon changed the name to sovereign.
Background and authorisation
The English sovereign, the country's first coin to be valued at one pound, was struck by the monarchs of the 16th century, the size and fineness often being altered.
Background and authorisation

Creation
William Wellesley Pole, elder brother of the Duke of Wellington, was appointed Master of the Mint (at that time a junior government position) in 1812, with a mandate to reform the Royal Mint.
Creation
Formal instruction to the Mint came with an indenture dated February 1817, directing the Royal Mint to strike gold sovereigns.
Creation
The Italian sculptor Benedetto Pistrucci came to London early in 1816.
Creation
In 1816, Pole hired Pistrucci to create models for the new coinage.
Creation
After completing Lady Spencer's commission, by most accounts, Pistrucci suggested to Pole that an appropriate subject for the sovereign would be Saint George.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
The original 1817 design had the saintly knight still carrying part of his broken spear.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
This was changed to a sword when the garter that originally surrounded the design was eliminated in 1821, and George is intended to have broken his spear earlier in the encounter with the dragon.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design

Pistrucci's George and Dragon design

The term sovereign, referring to a coin, fell from use—it does not appear in Samuel Johnson's dictionary, compiled in the 1750s.
Background and authorisation
After the war, Parliament, by the Coinage Act 1816, placed Britain officially on the gold standard, with the pound to be defined as a given quantity of gold.
Background and authorisation
A committee of the Privy Council recommended gold coins of ten shillings, twenty shillings, two pounds and five pounds be issued, and this was accepted by George, Prince Regent on 3 August 1816.
Creation
William Wellesley Pole, elder brother of the Duke of Wellington, was appointed Master of the Mint (at that time a junior government position) in 1812, with a mandate to reform the Royal Mint.
Creation
Formal instruction to the Mint came with an indenture dated February 1817, directing the Royal Mint to strike gold sovereigns.
Creation
The Italian sculptor Benedetto Pistrucci came to London early in 1816.
Creation
In 1816, Pole hired Pistrucci to create models for the new coinage.
Creation
After completing Lady Spencer's commission, by most accounts, Pistrucci suggested to Pole that an appropriate subject for the sovereign would be Saint George.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
The original 1817 design had the saintly knight still carrying part of his broken spear.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
This was changed to a sword when the garter that originally surrounded the design was eliminated in 1821, and George is intended to have broken his spear earlier in the encounter with the dragon.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
Also removed in 1821 was the plume of hair, or streamer, behind George's helmet; it was restored in 1887, modified in 1893 and 1902, and eliminated in 2009.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design

When Pistrucci created the coin, Neoclassicism was all the rage in London, and he may have been inspired by the Elgin Marbles, which were exhibited from 1807, and which he probably saw soon after his arrival in London.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design

Pistrucci's sovereign was unusual for a British coin of the 19th century in not having a heraldic design, but this was consistent with Pole's desire to make the sovereign look as different from the guinea as possible.
Early years (1817–1837)
When the sovereign entered circulation in late 1817, it was not initially popular, as the public preferred the convenience of the banknotes the sovereign had been intended to replace.
Early years (1817–1837)
Lack of demand meant that mintages dropped from 2,347,230 in 1818 to 3,574 the following year.
Early years (1817–1837)

Another reason why few sovereigns were struck in 1819 was a proposal, eventually rejected, by economist David Ricardo to eliminate gold as a coinage metal, though making it available on demand from the Bank of England.
Early years (1817–1837)
Once this plan was abandoned in 1820, the Bank encouraged the circulation of gold sovereigns, but acceptance among the British public was slow.
Early years (1817–1837)

The early sovereigns were heavily exported; in 1819, Robert Peel estimated that of the some £5,000,000 in gold struck in France since the previous year, three-quarters of the gold used had come from the new British coinage, melted down.
Early years (1817–1837)

Many more sovereigns were exported to France in the 1820s as the metal alloyed with the gold included silver, which could be profitably recovered, with the gold often returned to Britain and struck again into sovereigns.
Early years (1817–1837)
Beginning in 1829, the Mint was able to eliminate the silver, but the drain on sovereigns from before then continued.
Early years (1817–1837)
George III died in January 1820, succeeded by George, Prince Regent, as George IV.
Early years (1817–1837)
The new version was authorised by an Order in Council of 5 May 1821.
Early years (1817–1837)
Pistrucci refused to copy the work of another artist and was barred from further work on the coinage.
Early years (1817–1837)
Second Engraver (later Chief Engraver) William Wyon was assigned to translate Chantrey's bust into a coin design, and the new sovereign came into use during 1825.
Early years (1817–1837)
The George and Dragon design would not again appear on the sovereign until 1871.
Early years (1817–1837)
William IV 's accession in 1830 upon the death of his brother George IV led to new designs for the sovereign, with the new king's depiction engraved by William Wyon based on a bust by Chantrey.
Victorian era
The new coin was approved on 26 February 1838, and with the exception of 1840 and 1867, the "shield back" sovereign was struck at the Royal Mint in London every year from 1838 to 1874.
Victorian era
Sovereigns struck in London with the shield design between 1863 and 1874 bear small numbers under the shield, representing which coinage die was used.
Victorian era

By 1850, some £94 million in sovereigns and half sovereigns had been struck and circulated widely, well beyond Britain's shores, a dispersion aided by the British government, who saw the sovereign's use as an auxiliary to their imperialist ambitions.
Victorian era

In 1838, when the legacy of James Smithson was converted into gold in preparation for transmission to the United States, American authorities requested recently-struck sovereigns, likely to maximise the quantity of gold when the sovereigns were melted after arrival in the United States.
Victorian era
The weight of a newly-struck sovereign was intended to be 123.274 grains (7.98805 g).
Victorian era
It ceased to be legal currency for £1 if found to weigh less than 122 1 ⁄ 2 grains (i.e. a deficiency of 1 1 ⁄ 2 pence in gold per sovereign).
Victorian era
Between 1842 and 1845, the Bank withdrew and had recoined some £14 million in lightweight gold, about one-third the amount of that metal in circulation.
Victorian era
This not only kept the sovereign to standard, it probably removed most of the remaining guineas still in commerce.
Victorian era

The unlucky holder of a lightweight gold coin could only turn it in as bullion, would lose at least 1 1 ⁄ 2 pence because of the lightness and often had to pay an equal amount to cover the Bank of England's costs.
Victorian era

The California Gold Rush and other discoveries of the 1840s and 1850s boosted the amount of available gold and also the number of sovereigns struck, with £150 million in sovereigns and half sovereigns coined between 1850 and 1875.
Victorian era

The Coinage Act 1889 also authorised the Bank of England to redeem worn gold coins from before Victoria's reign, but on 22 November 1890 all gold coins from before her reign were called in by Royal Proclamation and demonetised effective 28 February 1891.
Victorian era
The sovereign was seen in fiction: in Dickens ' Oliver Twist, Mrs Bumble is paid £25 in sovereigns for her information.
Victorian era

Although many sovereigns were melted down for recoining on reaching a foreign land (as were those for the Smithsonian) it was regarded as a circulating coin in dozens of British colonies and even in nations such as Brazil and Portugal; the latter accepted it at a value of 4,500 reis.
Victorian era
The return of Saint George was approved by the Queen, and authorised by an Order in Council dated 14 January 1871.
Victorian era
The two designs were struck side by side in London from 1871 to 1874, and at the Australian branch mints until 1887, after which the Pistrucci design alone was used.
Victorian era
The saint returned to the rarely-struck two- and five-pound pieces in 1887, and was placed on the half sovereign in 1893.
Victorian era
Wyon's "Young head" of Queen Victoria for the sovereign's obverse was struck from 1838 until 1887, when it was replaced by the " Jubilee head " by Joseph Boehm.
Victorian era

Victoria's death in 1901 led to a new obverse for her son and successor, Edward VII by George William de Saulles, which began production in 1902; Edward's death in 1910 necessitated a new obverse for his son, George V by Bertram Mackennal.
Branch mint coinage
In 1853, an Order in Council approved the establishment of the Sydney Mint; the Melbourne Mint would follow in 1872, and the Perth Mint in 1899.
Branch mint coinage
The act which regulated currency in New South Wales came into force on 18 July 1855 and stipulated that the gold coins were to be called sovereigns and half sovereigns.
Branch mint coinage
It was not until 1908 that what is now the Royal Canadian Mint, in Ottawa, opened, and it struck sovereigns with the mint mark "C" from 1908 to 1919, except 1912 and 1915, each year in small numbers.
Branch mint coinage
Branch mints at Bombay (1918; mint mark "I") and Pretoria (1923–1932; mint mark "SA") also struck sovereigns.
Branch mint coinage
Melbourne and Perth stopped striking sovereigns after 1931, with Sydney having closed in 1926.
Branch mint coinage
The 1932 sovereigns struck at Pretoria were the last to be issued intended as currency at their face value.
Trade coin (1914–1979)

Churchill's successor, George Goschen, urged issuing banknotes to replace the gold coins, saying he preferred £20 million in gold in the Bank of England to thirty million sovereigns in the hands of the public.
Trade coin (1914–1979)

As Britain moved towards war in the July Crisis of 1914, many sought to convert Bank of England notes into gold, and the bank's reserves of the metal fell from £27 million on 29 July to £11 million on 1 August.
Trade coin (1914–1979)

Cullimore Allen, in his 1965 book on sovereigns, recalled meeting his first payroll after the change to banknotes, with the workers dubious about the banknotes and initially asking to be paid in gold.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
After the war, the sovereign did not return to commerce in Britain, with the pieces usually worth more as gold than as currency.
Trade coin (1914–1979)

In 1925, the Chancellor, Winston Churchill, secured the passage of the Gold Standard Act 1925, restoring Britain to that standard, but with gold to be kept in reserve rather than as a means of circulation.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
The effort failed—Churchill regarded it as the worst mistake of his life—but some lightweight sovereigns were melted and restruck dated 1925, and were released only later.
Trade coin (1914–1979)

With a bust of King Edward by Humphrey Paget and the date 1937, these sovereigns were not authorised by royal proclamation prior to Edward VIII's abdication in December 1936, and are considered pattern coins.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
Extremely rare, one sold in 2020 for £1,000,000, setting what was then a record (since broken) for a British coin.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
Sovereigns in proof condition dated 1937 were struck for Edward's brother and successor, George VI, also designed by Paget, the only sovereigns to bear George's effigy.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
The 1925-dated George V sovereign was restruck in 1949, 1951 and 1952, lowering the value of the original, of which only a few had hitherto been known.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
Sovereigns were struck in 1953, the coronation year of Elizabeth II, bearing the portrait of her by Mary Gillick, though the gold pieces were placed only in the major museums.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
A 1953 sovereign sold at auction in 2014 for £384,000.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
Elizabeth II sovereigns bearing Gillick's portrait were struck as bullion pieces between 1957 and 1959, and from 1962 to 1968.
Trade coin (1914–1979)

The counterfeiting problem was minimised by the striking of about 45,000,000 sovereigns by 1968, and efforts by Treasury solicitors which resulted in the sovereign's acceptance as legal tender by the highest courts of several European nations.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
The sovereign's role in popular culture continued: in the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Q issues James Bond with a briefcase, the handle of which contains 50 sovereigns.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
The last of the Gillick sovereigns had been struck in 1968; when production resumed in 1974, it was with a portrait by Arnold Machin.
Trade coin (1914–1979)
The last coin minted at Tower Hill, in 1975, was a sovereign.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
Striking of bullion sovereigns had been suspended after 1982, and so the Maklouf portrait, struck every year but 1989 until the end of 1997, is seen on the sovereign only in proof condition.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
In 1989, a commemorative sovereign, the first, was issued for the 500th anniversary of Henry VII's sovereign.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
The reverse of the 1489 piece depicts a double Tudor rose fronted by the royal arms; a similar design with updated arms graces the reverse of the 1989 sovereign.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
Ian Rank-Broadley designed the fourth bust of Elizabeth to be used on the sovereign, and this went into use in 1998 and was used until 2015.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
A special reverse design was used in 2002 for the Golden Jubilee, with an adaptation of the royal arms on a shield by Timothy Noad recalling the 19th-century "shield back" sovereigns.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
The years 2005 and 2012 (the latter, Elizabeth's Diamond Jubilee) saw interpretations of the George and Dragon design, the first by Noad, the later by Paul Day.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
Day’s design was used for the first strike-on-the-day sovereign which commemorated the jubilee.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
The most recent special designs, in 2016 and 2017, were only for collectors.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
The 2016 collector's piece, for Elizabeth's 90th birthday, has a one-year-only portrait of her on the obverse designed by James Butler.
Bullion and collectors coin (1979–present)
The 2017 collector's piece returned to Pistrucci's original design of 1817 for the modern sovereign's 200th birthday, with the Garter belt and motto.
Collecting, other use and tax treatment
Coin auction houses deal in rare sovereigns of earlier date, as do specialist dealers.
Collecting, other use and tax treatment

As well as the 1937 Edward VIII and 1953 Elizabeth II sovereigns, rare dates in the series include the 1819, and the 1863 piece with the number "827" on the obverse in place of William Wyon's initials.
Collecting, other use and tax treatment
Only 24,768 of the Adelaide Pound were struck; surviving specimens are rare and highly prized.
Collecting, other use and tax treatment
The sovereign itself has been the subject of commemoration; in 2005, the Perth Mint issued a gold coin with face value A$ 25, reproducing the reverse design of the pre-1871 Sydney Mint sovereigns.
Strike-on-the-Day
Strike-on-the-day pieces are limited edition coins, mostly sovereigns, that were struck by the Royal Mint on the specific day of the occasion celebrated.

wrld_1915_austria_4_ducat_restrike.title: Ducat
sents: lead
The ducat (/ ˈ d ʌ k ə t /) coin was used as a trade coin in Europe from the later Middle Ages to the 19th century.
lead

Its most familiar version, the gold ducat or sequin containing around 3.5 grams (0.11 troy ounces) of 98.6% fine gold, originated in Venice in 1284 and gained wide international acceptance over the centuries.
lead
Similarly named silver ducatons also existed.
lead
The gold ducat circulated along with the Florentine florin and preceded both the modern British pound sterling and the United States dollar.
Predecessors
The first issue of scyphate billon coins modelled on Byzantine trachea was made by King Roger II of Sicily as part of the Assizes of Ariano (1140).
Predecessors

The first issue bears the figure of Christ and the Latin inscription Sit tibi, Christe, datus, quem tu regis iste ducatus (meaning "O Christ, let this duchy, which you rule, be dedicated to you") on the obverse.
Gold ducat of Venice
In the 13th century, the Venetians imported goods from the East and sold them at a profit north of the Alps.
Gold ducat of Venice
In 1252 Florence and Genoa introduced the gold florin and genovino, respectively, both of 3.5 grams of 98.6% fine gold; the florin preceded the ducat as Western Europe's first standard gold coin.
Gold ducat of Venice
The Venetian ducat contained 3.545 grams of 99.47% fine gold, the highest purity medieval metallurgy could produce.
Gold ducat of Venice
The legend on the left identifies the saint as S M VENET, i.e.
Gold ducat of Venice
Saint Mark of Venice, and the legend on the right identifies the doge, with his title DVX in the field.
Gold ducat of Venice
The reverse legend is the same as on Roger II’s ducats.
Gold ducat of Venice
Succeeding doges of Venice continued striking ducats, changing only their name on the obverse.
Gold ducat of Venice
The ducat had a variable price versus the silver Venetian lira, reaching 6.2 lire or 124 soldi (shillings) by 1470.
Gold ducat of Venice
At that point a ducat worth 124 soldi emerged as a new silver-based unit of account for quoting salaries and costs.
Gold ducat of Venice
Continued depreciation in the silver currency during the 16th century, however, made the gold ducat worth more than 124 soldi.
Gold ducat of Venice
Leonardo Loredan extended the coinage with a half ducat and subsequent doges added a quarter, and various multiples up to 105 ducats.
Gold ducat of Venice
All of these coins continued to use the designs and weight standards of the original 1284 ducat.
Gold ducat of Venice
Even after dates became a common feature of western coinage, Venice struck ducats without them until Napoleon ended the Venetian Republic in 1797.
Adoption, 14th century
The Popes subsequently changed these designs, but continued to strike ducats of the same weight and size into the 16th century.
Adoption, 14th century
Most imitations of the Venetian ducat were made in the Levant, where Venice spent more money than it received.
Adoption, 14th century
The Knights of Saint John struck ducats with grand master Dieudonné de Gozon, 1346-1353, kneeling before Saint John on the obverse and an angel seated on the Sepulcher of Christ on the reverse.
Adoption, 14th century
Subsequent grand masters, however, found it expedient to copy the Venetian types more exactly, first at Rhodes and then on Malta.
Adoption, 14th century
Genoese traders went further; they struck ducats at Chios that could be distinguished from the Venetian originals only by their workmanship.
Adoption, 14th century
The rarity of ducats that Genoese traders struck at Mytilene, Phocaea, and Pera suggests that Venetians melted those they encountered.
Hungarian ducats
In Western Europe, Venice was an active trader but they sold more than they bought, thus giving the Florentine florin an early foothold in the Rhine river valley in 1354.
Hungarian ducats
However, this Rhenish florin or gulden was debased over the centuries, from 3.43 g fine gold in 1354, to 2.76 g fine gold by 1419, and to 2.503 g fine gold by 1559.
Hungarian ducats
After Henckels assassinated Amadeus Aba in 1311, Charles I of Hungary began a gold coinage exploiting ores of Aba's ancient gold mines.
Hungarian ducats

In light of the 15th century debasement of the Rhenish florin or goldgulden versus the original ducat, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V recognized this distinction in 1524 when he made ducats of the Venetian standard valid money in the Empire with a value 39% higher than the gulden.
Hungarian ducats
Hungary continued to strike ducats with 3.53133 grams of 98.6% fine gold.
Hungarian ducats
In 1470, Matthias Corvinus replaced the coat of arms by a Madonna.
Adoption, 15th and 16th centuries

In the 15th and 16th centuries, international traders in Western Europe shifted from the florin to the ducat as their preferred currency, with ducats often co-circulating with locally minted gold coins like the Rhenish guilder, French écu and Spanish escudo.
Adoption, 15th and 16th centuries
In 1497, Spain reformed its gold excelente into a copy of the ducat which was known as the ducado from 1504.
Adoption, 15th and 16th centuries
23¾ carats fine and slightly smaller than the Venetian ducat, each had about 3.484 g of pure gold and was reckoned as 375 maravedís, the typical unit of account at the time.
Adoption, 15th and 16th centuries
The Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian — I initiated his own currency reform, minting gold ducats in Austria from 1511.
Adoption, 15th and 16th centuries
Gold ducats and florins were established through the rest of the Holy Roman Empire by minting ordinances (Reichsmünzordnung) in 1524, 1559, and later.
Adoption, 15th and 16th centuries

The ducat weighed 3.49 grams and was 23⅔ carats fine (3.442 g of pure gold) and exchanged at a ratio of 8 ducats for 11 Rhenish florins, which weighed 3.25 grams and were 18½ carats fine (2.503 g of pure gold).
Adoption, 15th and 16th centuries
The German territories retained these standards until the 19th century.
Ducats of the Netherlands
The collapse of the government of Francis of Anjou in 1583, however, left them without a constitutional ruler to name on those coins.
Ducats of the Netherlands
At first, ducats of Hungarian type struck in the Netherlands had a standing figure on the obverse with the crown and battle axe that St.
Ducats of the Netherlands
Ladislaus carried on the Hungarian prototype, but naming him with a different legend.
Ducats of the Netherlands
The legend, CONCORDIA RES PARVÆ CRESCUNT, shortened in a variation of ways, says "by concord small things increase".
Silver ducaton
The silver ducaton commenced in the Italian states in the mid-16th century as a large coin of approximately 30 grams fine silver, worth slightly less than the gold ducat or sequin.
Decline
Use of the ducat waned from the 17th century with the minting of freshly-mined Latin American gold to Iberian standards like the Spanish doubloon and the Portuguese moidore.
Decline

In the 19th century ducats were progressively dropped as standard coin of several nations, most significantly the Latin Monetary Union of 1865 (France, Italy, Switzerland) and the Vienna Monetary Treaty of 1857 (German Confederation, Austria-Hungary).
Decline
By the 20th century ducats have transitioned from trade coin used in daily commerce to bullion coin for collectors and investors.
Decline
Austria continued to strike ducats until 1915, and has continued to restrike the last of them, including some four ducat coins illustrated here.
Decline
Around 1913, the gold ducat was worth the equivalent of "nine shillings and four pence sterling, or somewhat more than two dollars.
Ducat mints
The Austrian Mint still mints single and four-ducats, both dated 1915.
Ducat mints
Germany and the Holy Roman Empire; many cities, states and principalities before 1871.
Ducat mints
The Hungarian mint still mints commemorative coins with 2, 3, 4 and 6-ducats quality.
Ducat mints
Netherlands still issues golden and silver ducats having the same weight, composite and design when they were first minted in 1586.
Ducat mints
Before the Swiss unification, the Swiss also minted ducats, the most well known of which are the Zürich ducats.

wrld_1947_mexico_50_pesos_centenari.title: Penny (United States coin)
sents: lead
The cent, the United States of America one-cent coin (symbol: ¢), often called the " penny ", is a unit of currency equaling one-hundredth of a United States of America dollar.
lead

It has been the lowest face-value physical unit of U.S. currency since the abolition of the half-cent in 1857 (the abstract mill, which has never been minted, equal to a tenth of a cent, continues to see limited use in the fields of taxation and finance).
lead
The first U.S. cent was produced in 1787, and the cent has been issued primarily as a copper or copper-plated coin throughout its history.
lead
Due to inflation, pennies have lost virtually all their purchasing power and are often viewed as an expensive burden to businesses, banks, government (especially mints) and the public in general.
lead
The penny is issued in its current form as the Lincoln cent, with its obverse featuring the profile of President Abraham Lincoln since 1909, the centennial of his birth.
lead
From 1959 (the sesquicentennial of Lincoln's birth) to 2008, the reverse featured the Lincoln Memorial.
lead
Four different reverse designs in 2009 honored Lincoln's 200th birthday and a new, "permanent" reverse – the Union Shield – was introduced in 2010.
lead
The coin is 0.75 inches (19.05 mm) in diameter and 0.0598 inches (1.52 mm) in thickness.
History of composition

The isotope composition of early coins spanning the period 1828 to 1843 reflects the copper from Cornish ores from England, while coins after 1850 reflect the Keweenaw Peninsula, Michigan ores, a finding consistent with historical records.
History of composition
In 1943, at the peak of World War II, zinc-coated steel cents were made for a short time because of war demands for copper.
History of composition
A few copper cents from 1943 were produced from 1942 planchets remaining in the bins.
History of composition

From 1944 to 1946, salvaged ammunition shells made their way into the minting process, and it was not uncommon to see coins featuring streaks of brass or having a considerably darker finish than other issues.
History of composition
During the early 1970s, the price of copper rose to the point where the cent contained almost one cent's worth of copper.
History of composition
Aluminum was chosen, and over 1.5 million samples of the 1974 aluminum cent were struck before ultimately being rejected.
History of composition
The cent's composition was changed in 1982 because the value of the copper in the coin started to rise above one cent.
History of composition
Some 1982 cents used the 97.5% zinc composition, while others used the 95% copper composition.
History of composition
With the exception of 2009 bicentennial cents minted specifically for collectors, United States cents minted after 1982 have been zinc with copper plating.
History of composition
In addition, a full 50-cent roll of pre-1982/3 coins weighs 5.4 oz (150 g) compared to a post-1982–83 roll which weighs 4.4 oz (120 g).
Designs
Until 1857 it was about the size of the current U.S. dollar coins (Susan B.
Designs
Throughout its history, the Lincoln cent has featured several typefaces for the date, but most of the digits have been old-style numerals, except with the 4 and 8 neither ascending nor descending.
Designs

The only significant divergence is that the small 3 was non-descending (the same size as a 0, 1, or 2) in the early history, before switching to a descending, large 3 for the year 1934 and then permanently (as of 2014) in 1943.
Designs
Similarly, the digit 5 was small and non-descending up to 1945.
Lincoln cent
It was adopted in 1909 (which would have been Lincoln's 100th birthday), replacing the Indian Head cent.
History

When the Lincoln one-cent coin made its initial appearance in 1909, it marked a radical departure from the accepted styling of United States coinage, as it was the first regular coin to bear a portrait other than the mythical Liberty which appeared on most pre-1909 regular coins.
History
Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th U.S. president, thought American coins were so common and uninspiring that he attempted to get the motto "In God We Trust" removed as offending religion.
History

Roosevelt, who considered Lincoln the savior of the Union and the greatest Republican president, and who also considered himself Lincoln's political heir, ordered the new Lincoln cent to be based on Brenner's work and to be released just in time to commemorate Lincoln's 100th birthday in 1909.
History
The United States Congress passed the Act of March 3, 1865, authorizing the use of this motto on U.S. coins, during Lincoln's tenure in office.
History
Franklin MacVeagh gave his approval on July 14, 1909, and not quite three weeks later, on August 2, the new coin was released to the public.
History
In 1918, after the controversy over Brenner's name and initials on the reverse had died down, his initials were placed on the obverse with no further controversy.
Wheat cent (1909–1958)
Thus in 1909 the U.S. had six different cents: the 1909 and 1909-S Indian Head cents, and four Lincoln coins: 1909 VDB, 1909-S VDB, 1909 and 1909-S.
Wheat cent (1909–1958)
While the smallest mintage is the '09-S Indian, the '09-S VDB is the key Lincoln date, and hence is most valuable.
Wheat cent (1909–1958)
Its mintage of 484,000 is only 1.7% of the plain V.D.B.
Lincoln Memorial cent (1959–2008)
On February 12, 1959, a revised reverse design was introduced as part of the 150th anniversary of Lincoln's birth.
Lincoln Memorial cent (1959–2008)

Frank Gasparro, then Assistant Engraver at the Philadelphia Mint, prepared the winning entry, selected from a group of 23 models that the engraving staff at the Mint had been asked to present for consideration.
Lincoln Memorial cent (1959–2008)
Again, only the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury was necessary to make the change because the design had been in use for more than the required 25 years.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
The Presidential $1 Coin Act of 2005 required that the cent's reverse be redesigned in 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Birth and early childhood in Kentucky: this design features a log cabin and Lincoln's birth year 1809.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
This cent was released into circulation on Lincoln's 200th birthday, February 12, 2009, at a special ceremony at LaRue County High School in Hodgenville, Kentucky, Lincoln's birthplace.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Nicknamed the "Indiana Penny", it was released on May 14, 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Nicknamed the "Illinois Penny", it was released on August 13, 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
This fourth cent was released to the public on November 12, 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Special 2009 cents struck for sale in sets to collectors had the metallic copper content of cents minted in 1909 (95% copper, 5% tin and zinc).
Union shield cent (2010–present)
Eighteen designs were proposed for the reverse of the 2010 cent.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
On April 16, 2009, the Commission of Fine Arts (CFA) met and selected a design that showed 13 wheat sheaves bound together with a ring symbolizing American unity as one nation.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
Later this design was withdrawn because it was similar to coinage issued in Germany in the 1920s.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
In June 2009 the CFA met again and chose a design featuring a modern rendition of the American flag.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
As a part of the release ceremony for the last of the 2009 cents on November 12, the design for the 2010 cent was announced.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
According to the Mint, the 13 stripes on the shield "represent the states joined in one compact union to support the Federal government, represented by the horizontal bar above".
Union shield cent (2010–present)
The new Union Shield design replaces the Lincoln memorial in use since 1959.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
In January 2010, the coins were released early in Puerto Rico; this was caused by a shortage of 2009-dated pennies on the island.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
The new design was released at a ceremony at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library in Springfield, Illinois on February 11, 2010.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
In 2017, cents minted in Philadelphia were struck with a "P" mintmark to celebrate the 225th anniversary of the U.S.

The ruble or rouble (Russian: рубль, romanized: rublʹ; symbol: ₽; abbreviation: руб or р. in Cyrillic, Rub in Latin; ISO code: RUB) is the currency of the Russian Federation.
lead

lead
It is used in Russia as well as in the parts of Ukraine under Russian military occupation and in Russian-occupied parts of Georgia.
lead
The ruble was the currency of the Russian Empire and of the Soviet Union (as the Soviet ruble).
lead
In 1992, the currency imagery underwent a redesign as a result of the fall of the Soviet Union.
lead

lead

History
The ruble has been used in the Russian territories since the 14th century, and is the second-oldest currency still in circulation, behind sterling.
History
Initially an uncoined unit of account, the ruble became a circulating coin in 1704 just before the establishment of the Russian Empire.
History
It was also the first currency in Europe to be decimalised in 1704, when it was divided into 100 kopecks.
Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, the Soviet ruble remained the currency of the Russian Federation until 1992.
A new set of coins was issued in 1992 and a new set of banknotes was issued in the name of Bank of Russia in 1993.
The currency replaced the Soviet ruble at par and was assigned the ISO 4217 code RUR and number 810.

After the fall of the Soviet Union, the Russian Federation introduced new coins in 1992 in denominations of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 rubles.

The coins depict the double-headed eagle without a crown, sceptre and globus cruciger above the legend "Банк России" ("Bank of Russia").
RUR coins

As high inflation persisted, the lowest denominations disappeared from circulation and the other denominations became rarely used.

All Soviet coins issued between 1961 and 1991, as well as 1-, 2- and 3-kopeck coins issued before 1961, also qualified for exchange into new rubles.

The ruble was subject to fluctuation when, in April 2022, the ruble went above its pre- war level after falling as low as 150 ₽ per dollar in early March, with the longer-term trend showing a steady decline from mid-2022 to mid-2023, falling from 60 ₽ to 90 ₽ per dollar.

On 15 July 2024 the Central Bank of the Russian Federation closed the statistics of the over-the-counter currency market, and three days later the sale of ruble-note artwork on toilet paper was banned by a judge from Moscow.

Modifications to the series were made in 2001, 2004, and 2010.

The 2,000 ₽ banknote will bear images of the Russian Far East: the bridge to Russky Island and the Vostochny Cosmodrome in the Amur Oblast.

In 2018, the Central Bank issued a 100 ₽ "commemorative" banknote designed to recognize Russia's role as the host of the 2018 World Cup soccer tournament.

Despite the note being intended for legal tender transactions, the Central Bank has simultaneously refused to allow the country's automated teller machines (ATMs) to recognize or accept it.

Commemorative banknotes

On the reverse there is the number 2018 that marks both the issue of the banknote and the World Cup, as well as the name of the host cities in the Russian language.

The use of other currencies for transactions between Russian residents is punishable, with a few exceptions, with a fine of 75% to 100% of the value of the transaction.

The Mexican peso (symbol: $; currency code: MXN; also abbreviated Mex$ to distinguish it from other peso-denominated currencies; referred to as the peso, Mexican peso, or colloquially varo) is the official currency of Mexico.

lead
The Mexican peso is subdivided into 100 centavos, represented by " ¢ ".
lead
Mexican banknotes are issued by the Bank of Mexico in various denominations and feature vibrant colors and imagery representing Mexican culture and history.
lead

lead
Prior to the 1993 revaluation, the code MXP was used.
lead

The Mexican peso is the 16th most traded currency in the world, the third most traded currency from the Americas (after the United States dollar and Canadian dollar), and the most traded currency from Latin America.
Precursor
15 or 16 silver reales were worth a gold escudo, and eight-real coins of 24.44 g fine silver were widely called pesos in Spanish America and dollars in Britain and its American colonies.
Precursor
Mexican silver pesos of original cap-and-ray design were legal tender in the United States until 1857 and in China until 1935.

The post-independence silver peso contained 27.07 grams of 90.3% fine silver (24.44 g fine) while the gold peso or half escudo contained 1.6915 grams of 87.5% fine gold (1.48 g fine).
Origin

After most of Europe switched to the gold standard in the 1870s the gold peso substantially rose in value against the silver peso, until it became 2 silver pesos to a gold peso or a gold peso dollar by 1900.
Origin
From 1918 onward the weight and fineness of all the silver coins declined, until 1979, when the last silver 100-peso coins were minted.
Origin
The U.S. dollar was worth 2.00 silver pesos from 1905 to 1929, rising afterward until it stabilized at 12.50 pesos from 1954 to 1976.
Reformation

Throughout most of the 20th century, the Mexican peso remained one of the more stable currencies in Latin America, since the economy did not experience periods of hyperinflation common to other countries in the region.

The U.S. dollar leapt from 12.50 to 19.40 pesos in 1976.

The government's operational balances had been predicted to remain stable as the country was operating in a surplus between 1990 and 1994.

A revised $50 note, with improved security features, was released on May 6, 2013, and is known as Type F1.
Commemorative banknotes
The 100-peso denomination note commemorates the centennial of the Beginning of the Mexican Revolution (1910–1920).
Commemorative banknotes
Likewise, a 100-peso banknote that commemorates the 100th anniversary of the enactment of the Constitution of Mexico was unveiled and issued in 2017.
Commemorative banknotes

In 2019, the Bank of Mexico issued a new 200-peso banknote of the Series G issues, but containing a special overprint referencing the 25th Anniversary of the Bank of Mexico's Autonomy from the Federal Government.
Series G

This series was not originally intended to include a $20 note, since it would gradually be replaced by a coin, but a $20 note to commemorate the bicentennial of Mexican independence was issued in September 2021.
Series G
The 20, 50, and 100-peso notes are produced in polymer, while the other banknotes are printed on paper.
Series G
Should there be a need, Banco de México will introduce a $2,000 note.
Series G
200-peso notes have two lines; 500 and 1000-peso notes have three and four, respectively.
Series G
The value of the 20, 50, and 100-peso notes are embossed in the clear windows of the corresponding notes, along with a distinctive pattern.
19th century

The first U.S. dollar coins were not issued until April 2, 1792, and the peso continued to be officially recognized and used in the United States, along with other foreign coins, until February 21, 1857.

wrld_1898_mexico_cap_and_rays_8_rea.title: Spanish dollar
sents: lead

The Spanish dollar, also known as the piece of eight (Spanish: real de a ocho, dólar, peso duro, peso fuerte or peso), is a silver coin of approximately 38 mm (1.5 in) diameter worth eight Spanish reales.
lead
It was minted in the Spanish Empire following a monetary reform in 1497 with content 25.563 g (0.8219 ozt) fine silver.
lead
It was widely used as the first international currency because of its uniformity in standard and milling characteristics.
lead
Some countries countermarked the Spanish dollar so it could be used as their local currency.
lead
Because the Spanish dollar was widely used in Europe, the Americas, and the Far East, it became the first world currency by the 16th century.
lead

The Spanish dollar was the coin upon which the original United States dollar was based (at 0.7735 troy ounces or 24.06 grams), and it remained legal tender in the United States until the Coinage Act of 1857.
lead
Many other currencies around the world, such as the Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan, were initially based on the Spanish dollar and other 8-real coins.
lead
Most theories trace the origin of the "$" symbol, which originally had two vertical bars, to the pillars of Hercules wrapped in ribbons that appear on the reverse side of the Spanish dollar.
Etymology
In the 16th century, Count Hieronymus Schlick of Bohemia began minting a silver coin known as a Joachimsthaler, named after Joachimsthal, the valley in the Ore Mountains where the silver was mined.
Europe and colonial North America
The Joachimsthaler weighed 451 Troy grains (29.2 g; 0.94 ozt) of silver.
Europe and colonial North America

The Netherlands also introduced its own dollars in the 16th century: the Burgundian Cross Thaler (Bourgondrische Kruisdaalder), the German-inspired Rijksdaalder, and the Dutch lion dollar (leeuwendaalder).
Europe and colonial North America
For the English North American colonists, however, the Spanish peso or "piece of eight" has always held first place, and this coin was also called the "dollar" as early as 1581.
Spain

After the introduction of the Guldengroschen in Austria in 1486, the concept of a large silver coin with high purity (sometimes known as "specie" coinage) eventually spread throughout the rest of Europe.
Spain
This was supplemented in 1537 by the gold escudo, minted at 68 to a mark of gold 0.917 fine (fineness reduced to 0.906 in 1742 and 0.875 in 1786).
Spain
It was valued at 15–16 reales or approximately 2 dollars.
Spain
The famed Gold Doubloon was worth 2 escudos or approximately 4 dollars.
Spain
From the 15th to the 19th centuries the coin was minted with several different designs at various mints in Spain and the New World, having gained wide acceptance beyond Spain's borders.
Spain
The dollar or peso was divided into 8 reales in Spanish Latin America until the 19th century when the peso was divided into 100 centavos.
Spain
Spain's adoption of the peseta in 1869 and its joining the Latin Monetary Union meant the effective end of the last vestiges of the Spanish dollar in Spain itself.
Spain
However, the 5-peseta coin (or duro) was slightly smaller and lighter but was also of high purity (90%) silver.
Spain
In the 1990s, commemorative 2,000-peseta coins were minted, similar in size and weight to the dollar.
Mexico
Following independence in 1821, Mexican coinage of silver reales and gold escudos followed that of Spanish lines until decimalization and the introduction of the peso worth 8 reales or 100 centavos.
Mexico

It continued to be minted to Spanish standards throughout the 19th century, with the peso at 27.07 grams (0.955 oz) of 0.9028 fine silver, and the escudo at 3.383 grams (0.1193 oz) of 0.875 fine gold.
Mexico
The Mexican peso or 8-real coin continued to be a popular international trading coin throughout the 19th century.
Mexico
After 1918, the peso was reduced in size and fineness, with further reductions in the 1940s and 1950s.
Mexico
However, 2- (1921), 5- (1947) and 10-peso (1955) coins were minted during the same period with sizes and fineness similar to the old peso.
Australia

After the colony of New South Wales was founded in Australia in 1788, it ran into the problem of a lack of coinage, particularly since trading vessels took coins out of the colony in exchange for their cargo.
Australia
In 1813, Governor Lachlan Macquarie made creative use of £10,000 in Spanish dollars sent by the British government.
Australia
The punched centre, known as the "dump", was valued at 15 pence, and the outer rim, known as the " holey dollar ", was worth five shillings.
Australia
The obverse of the holey dollar was stamped the words "New South Wales" and the date, 1813, and the reverse with the words "five shillings".
Australia
The obverse of the dump was stamped with a crown, the words "New South Wales" and the date, 1813, and the reverse with the words "fifteen pence".
Australia
The mutilated coins became the first official currency produced specifically for circulation in Australia.
Australia

The British Parliament passed the Sterling Silver Money Act in 1825, which made British coins the only recognised form of currency and ended any legitimate use of the holey dollar and dump in the Australian colonies.
United States
By far the leading specie coin circulating in America was the Spanish silver dollar, defined as consisting of 387 grains of pure silver.
United States
The Spanish silver dollar had been the world's outstanding coin since the early 16th century, and was spread partially by dint of the vast silver output of the Spanish colonies in Latin America.
United States
More important, however, was that the Spanish dollar, from the 16th to the 19th century, was relatively the most stable and least debased coin in the Western world.
United States
The Coinage Act of 1792 specified that the U.S. dollar would contain 371.25 grains (24.057 g) pure or 416 grains (26.96 g) standard silver.
United States
Initially this dollar was comparable to the 371–373 grains found in circulating Spanish dollars and aided in its exportation overseas.
United States
The restoration of the old 0.9028 fineness in the Mexican peso after 1821, however, increased the latter's silver content to 24.44 g and reduced the export demand for U.S. dollars.
United States
Spanish coinage was legal tender in the United States until the Coinage Act of 1857 discontinued the practice.
United States

The pricing of equities on U.S. stock exchanges in 1 ⁄ 8 -dollar denominations persisted until the New York Stock Exchange converted first to pricing in sixteenths of a dollar on 24 June 1997, and then in 2001 to decimal pricing.
Asia
The first Chinese yuan coins had the same specification as a Spanish dollar, leading to a continuing equivalence in some respects between the names "yuan" and "dollar" in the Chinese language.
Fiction
In modern pop culture and fiction, pieces of eight are most often associated with the popular notion of pirates.
Fiction

In the film Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End the Pirate Lords must meet together by presenting the "Nine Pieces of Eight", since these Pieces were used to seal the goddess Calypso in her human form by the first Brethren Court.
Fiction
Pieces of Eight is the eighth studio album and second concept album by Styx, released on 1 September 1978.

wrld_1890_great_britain_victoria_cr.title: Crown (British coin)

Design: Profile of the monarch (Victoria "jubilee head" design shown)

sents: lead
The crown was a denomination of sterling coinage worth 1 ⁄ 4 of one pound, or 5 shillings, or 60 (old) pence.
lead
The crown was first issued during the reign of Edward VI, as part of the coinage of the Kingdom of England.
lead

Always a heavy silver coin weighing around one ounce, during the 19th and 20th centuries the crown declined from being a real means of exchange to being a coin rarely spent, and minted for commemorative purposes only.
lead
Unlike in some territories of the British Empire (such as Jamaica), in the UK the crown was never replaced as circulating currency by a five-shilling banknote.
lead
"Decimal" crowns were minted a few times after decimalisation of the British currency in 1971, initially with a nominal value of 25 (new) pence.
lead
However, commemorative crowns issued since 1990 have a face value of five pounds.
History

The coin's origins lie in the English silver crown, one of many silver coins that appeared in various countries from the 16th century onwards (most famously the Spanish piece of eight), all of similar size and weight (approx 38mm diameter, 25g fine silver) and thus interchangeable in international trade.
History
The dies for all gold and silver coins of Queen Anne and King George I were engraved by John Croker, a migrant originally from Dresden in the Duchy of Saxony.
History
The British silver crown was always a large coin, and from the 19th century it did not circulate well.
History

The King George V "wreath" crowns struck from 1927 through 1936 (excluding 1935 when the more common "rocking horse" crown was minted to commemorate the King's Silver Jubilee) depict a wreath on the reverse of the coin and were struck in very low numbers.
History
The 1927 "wreath" crowns were struck as proofs only (15,030 minted) and the 1934 coin had a mintage of just 932.
History
The 1951 issue was for the Festival of Britain, and was only struck in proof condition.
History

The 1953 crown was issued to celebrate the Coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, while the 1960 issue (which carried the same reverse design as the previous crown in 1953) commemorated the British Exhibition in New York.
History
The 1965 issue carried the image of Winston Churchill on the reverse.
History

According to the Standard Catalogue of coins, 19,640,000 of this coin were minted, although intended as collectable pieces the large mintage and lack of precious metal content means these coins are effectively worthless today.
History
Production of the Churchill crown began on 11 October 1965, and stopped in the summer of 1966.
History
The crown coin was nicknamed the dollar, as one United States dollar on the gold standard was worth about the same (slightly less).
History
In 2014, a new world record price was achieved for a milled silver crown.
History
The coin was unique, issued as a pattern by engraver Thomas Simon in 1663 and nicknamed the "Reddite Crown".
History
Auctioneers Spink & Son of London sold the coin on 27 March 2014 for £396,000 including commission.
History
All pre-decimal crowns from 1818 on remain legal tender with a face value of 25p.
Decimal crowns
After decimalisation on 15 February 1971, the 25-pence coin was introduced as a replacement for the crown as a commemorative coin.
Decimal crowns
From 1990, the face value of new crown coins was raised to five pounds.
Changing values
The legal tender value of the crown remained as five shillings from 1544 to 1965.
Changing values
From 1927 to 1939, the word "CROWN" appears, and from 1951 to 1960 this was changed to "FIVE SHILLINGS".
Changing values
Coins minted since 1818 remain legal tender with a face value of 25 pence.
Changing values

Although all "normal" issues since 1951 have been composed of cupro-nickel, special proof versions have been produced for sale to collectors, and as gift items, in silver, gold, and occasionally platinum.
Changing values

The fact that gold £5 crowns are now produced means that there are two different strains of five pound gold coins, namely crowns and what are now termed "quintuple sovereigns" for want of a more concise term.
Changing values
Numismatically, the term "crown-sized" is used generically to describe large silver or cupro-nickel coins of about 40 mm in diameter.
Changing values
Most Commonwealth countries still issue crown-sized coins for sale to collectors.
Composition
For silver crowns, the grade of silver adhered to the long-standing standard (established in the 12th century by Henry II) – the Sterling Silver standard of 92.5% silver and 7.5% copper.
Composition

In a debasement process which took effect in 1920, the silver content of all British coins was reduced from 92.5% to 50%, with a portion of the remainder consisting of manganese, which caused the coins to tarnish to a very dark colour after they had been in circulation for a significant period.
Composition
Silver was eliminated altogether in 1947, with the move to a composition of cupro-nickel – except for proof issues, which returned to the pre-1920 92.5% silver composition.
Composition
Since the Great Recoinage of 1816, a crown has, as a general rule, had a diameter of 38.61 millimetres (1.520 in), and weighed 28.276 grams (defined as 10 ⁄ 11 troy ounce).
Quarter sovereign

In 1853, the Royal Mint had produced two patterns for a gold 5-shilling coin for circulation use, one denominated as five shillings and the other as a quarter sovereign, but this coin never went into production, in part due to concerns about the small size of the coin and likely wear in circulation.
Quarter sovereign
The quarter sovereign was introduced in 2009 as a bullion coin.

wrld_1938_canada_silver_dollar.title: Canadian silver dollar
sents: lead
The Canadian silver dollar (French: Dollar argent du Canada) was first issued by the Royal Canadian Mint in 1935 to commemorate the Silver Jubilee of King George V.
lead
The coin's reverse design was sculpted by Emanuel Hahn and portrays a voyageur and a person of Indigenous descent paddling a birch-bark canoe.
lead
The faint lines in the background represent the Northern Lights.
lead
The voyageur design was used on the dollar until 1986.
lead
It was then replaced with the 1987 Canadian 1-dollar coin (colloquially known as the "loonie").
lead
1967 marked the end of the silver dollar as a business strike, or a coin issued for circulation.
lead
After 1967, the dollar coin was made of nickel, except for non-circulating commemorative issues for the collector market, which continue to contain silver.
While the silver dollar was not struck for production in 1911, three trial strikes were produced by the Royal Mint in London: two struck in silver and one in lead.
Since these coins were unique and not intended for circulation, they have been classified as pattern coins.
One of the silver coins, owned by the Royal Mint Museum, has been loaned to the Bank of Canada since 1976 and has been displayed in the Bank of Canada Museum since 1980.
The lead coin was not discovered until 1977, during an office move from Parliament Hill.
The second 1911 silver dollar had belonged to William Ellison-Macartney, deputy mint master of the Royal Mint.
After he died in 1924, the coin was passed on to his three children, before eventually being sold to Blair A.
The coin was eventually sold in 1965 to John McKay-Clements, former mayor of Haileybury, Ontario.
Following McKay-Clements' death in 1976, the coin was auctioned off again.
Due to its uniqueness, it gained the nickname of the "Emperor of Canadian Coins" around the same time the 1911 half-dollar was dubbed the "King of Canadian Coins".

The coin changed hands several more times, being sold to Anthony Carrato of Eagle Coin Company for US$160,000 in July 1979, then Joseph Carlton and David Hirschman of Carlton Numismatics Inc. for US$325,000.
Eventually, the coin made its way back to Canada after being auctioned off for US$690,000 to George H.
Cook, a renowned Canadian collector, on January 13, 2003.

After his death in 2018, Cook's collection was auctioned off during the American Numismatic Association World's Fair of Money in Chicago, where it was bought one final time by Sandy Campbell and Ian Laing for $734,000 after a 20% buyer's fee.
As part of the National Currency Collection, it rejoined its silver twin and lead counterpart for the first time in nearly 110 years since their mintage.
Pointed seven
Two styles of the number 7 in 1947 were used in the dies to produce the Voyageur coins.
Pointed seven
Pointed 7 with a quadruple punched HP under the effigy of His Majesty King George VI (The HP is the initials of the designer: T.H.
Blunt seven
A shorter 7 with the lower tail pointing almost straight down has been labelled as the blunt seven.
Maple Leaf issue
In 1947, India gained its independence from the British Empire and as a result, the inscription "IND:IMP:" needed to be removed from the Obverse of the 1948 Silver Dollar.
Maple Leaf issue

However, because there was a delay in new master dies being shipped from the UK to reflect this change, the Mint continued to produce 1947 year coins with a small Maple Leaf by the date to denote they were actually minted in 1948.
Maple Leaf issue
Eventually the new Obverse dies did arrive, and they began to mint the 1948 dollars midway through the year.
Maple Leaf issue
The very low mintages of these made the 1947 Maple Leaf and 1948 dollars exceptionally rare, with the 1948 Silver Dollar commanding a very high market price.
Arnprior type varieties
A technical problem emanated during the 1950s that was to plague the Royal Canadian Mint.
Arnprior type varieties

There were collectors that decided arbitrarily that a certain pattern of partial water lines at the right-hand end of the canoe should be collected separately and command a premium over dollars with perfect water lines or other partial lines configurations.
Arnprior type varieties
The Arnprior type configurations tended to consist of 2 and ½ water lines at the right.
Varieties of 1952
A modified reverse, with no water lines at all, was put into use in 1952.
Origin of the Arnprior name
In December 1955, the Royal Canadian Mint made up an order of 2,000 silver dollars for a firm in Arnprior, Ontario.
Origin of the Arnprior name
This was similar to the accidental disappearance of water lines on the versions from 1950 to 1951.
Origin of the Arnprior name
The 1955 dollars caught the interest of many collectors and it was this version that led to the term Arnprior being applied to any dollar with an appearance of missing water lines.
Origin of the Arnprior name
An even more collectible of the 1955 Arnprior, is given by the die break on the obverse legend, with the result being the joining of the T and the I in GRATIA.
No shoulder fold obverse
An element that was common in every denomination of 1953 was the two obverses that existed.
1957 Arnprior
The 1957 dollar had a reverse that was considered an Arnprior.
Although 1965 would mark a change in the effigy of Queen Elizabeth II, the year would offer five different varieties of the dollar.
Variety 1 and 2
The small beads on the obverse of the coin define varieties 1 and 2.
Variety 1 and 2
There is a pointed 5 (the point is at the bottom) while there is another version with a blunt 5 (the bluntness is at the bottom of the 5 too).
Variety 3 and 4
The large beads on the obverse of the coin define varieties 3 and 4.
Variety 3 and 4
There is a pointed 5 (the point is at the bottom) while there is another version with a blunt 5 (the bluntness is at the bottom of the 5 too).
Variety 5
Unlike the other varieties, the 5 in 1965 is pointed.
1982 planchet varieties
The normal planchet has a weight of 15.62 grams, a diameter of 32.13 mm, and a thickness of 2.50 mm.
1982 planchet varieties
Its weight is 7.78 grams, a diameter of 31.82 mm, and a thickness of 1.50 mm.
Note: 1981 was the first year that the RCM issued two different qualities of silver dollars.
