The cent's composition was changed in 1982 because the value of the copper in the coin started to rise above one cent.
History of composition
Some 1982 cents used the 97.5% zinc composition, while others used the 95% copper composition.
History of composition
With the exception of 2009 bicentennial cents minted specifically for collectors, United States cents minted after 1982 have been zinc with copper plating.
History of composition
In addition, a full 50-cent roll of pre-1982/3 coins weighs 5.4 oz (150 g) compared to a post-1982–83 roll which weighs 4.4 oz (120 g).
Designs
Until 1857 it was about the size of the current U.S. dollar coins (Susan B.
Designs
Throughout its history, the Lincoln cent has featured several typefaces for the date, but most of the digits have been old-style numerals, except with the 4 and 8 neither ascending nor descending.
Designs

The only significant divergence is that the small 3 was non-descending (the same size as a 0, 1, or 2) in the early history, before switching to a descending, large 3 for the year 1934 and then permanently (as of 2014) in 1943.
Designs
Similarly, the digit 5 was small and non-descending up to 1945.
Lincoln cent
It was adopted in 1909 (which would have been Lincoln's 100th birthday), replacing the Indian Head cent.
History

When the Lincoln one-cent coin made its initial appearance in 1909, it marked a radical departure from the accepted styling of United States coinage, as it was the first regular coin to bear a portrait other than the mythical Liberty which appeared on most pre-1909 regular coins.
History
Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th U.S. president, thought American coins were so common and uninspiring that he attempted to get the motto "In God We Trust" removed as offending religion.
History

Roosevelt, who considered Lincoln the savior of the Union and the greatest Republican president, and who also considered himself Lincoln's political heir, ordered the new Lincoln cent to be based on Brenner's work and to be released just in time to commemorate Lincoln's 100th birthday in 1909.
History
The United States Congress passed the Act of March 3, 1865, authorizing the use of this motto on U.S. coins, during Lincoln's tenure in office.
History
Franklin MacVeagh gave his approval on July 14, 1909, and not quite three weeks later, on August 2, the new coin was released to the public.
History
In 1918, after the controversy over Brenner's name and initials on the reverse had died down, his initials were placed on the obverse with no further controversy.
Wheat cent (1909–1958)
Thus in 1909 the U.S. had six different cents: the 1909 and 1909-S Indian Head cents, and four Lincoln coins: 1909 VDB, 1909-S VDB, 1909 and 1909-S.
Wheat cent (1909–1958)
While the smallest mintage is the '09-S Indian, the '09-S VDB is the key Lincoln date, and hence is most valuable.
Wheat cent (1909–1958)
Its mintage of 484,000 is only 1.7% of the plain V.D.B.
Lincoln Memorial cent (1959–2008)
On February 12, 1959, a revised reverse design was introduced as part of the 150th anniversary of Lincoln's birth.
Lincoln Memorial cent (1959–2008)

Frank Gasparro, then Assistant Engraver at the Philadelphia Mint, prepared the winning entry, selected from a group of 23 models that the engraving staff at the Mint had been asked to present for consideration.
Lincoln Memorial cent (1959–2008)
Again, only the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury was necessary to make the change because the design had been in use for more than the required 25 years.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
The Presidential $1 Coin Act of 2005 required that the cent's reverse be redesigned in 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Birth and early childhood in Kentucky: this design features a log cabin and Lincoln's birth year 1809.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
This cent was released into circulation on Lincoln's 200th birthday, February 12, 2009, at a special ceremony at LaRue County High School in Hodgenville, Kentucky, Lincoln's birthplace.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Nicknamed the "Indiana Penny", it was released on May 14, 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Nicknamed the "Illinois Penny", it was released on August 13, 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
This fourth cent was released to the public on November 12, 2009.
Lincoln Bicentennial cents (2009)
Special 2009 cents struck for sale in sets to collectors had the metallic copper content of cents minted in 1909 (95% copper, 5% tin and zinc).
Union shield cent (2010–present)
Eighteen designs were proposed for the reverse of the 2010 cent.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
On April 16, 2009, the Commission of Fine Arts (CFA) met and selected a design that showed 13 wheat sheaves bound together with a ring symbolizing American unity as one nation.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
Later this design was withdrawn because it was similar to coinage issued in Germany in the 1920s.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
In June 2009 the CFA met again and chose a design featuring a modern rendition of the American flag.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
As a part of the release ceremony for the last of the 2009 cents on November 12, the design for the 2010 cent was announced.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
According to the Mint, the 13 stripes on the shield "represent the states joined in one compact union to support the Federal government, represented by the horizontal bar above".
Union shield cent (2010–present)
The new Union Shield design replaces the Lincoln memorial in use since 1959.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
In January 2010, the coins were released early in Puerto Rico; this was caused by a shortage of 2009-dated pennies on the island.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
The new design was released at a ceremony at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library in Springfield, Illinois on February 11, 2010.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
In 2017, cents minted in Philadelphia were struck with a "P" mintmark to celebrate the 225th anniversary of the U.S.
Union shield cent (2010–present)
2017 is the only year that Philadelphia cents have had a mintmark.
Union shield cent (2010–present)

In 2019, the United States Mint, the West Point Mint minted pennies marked with a "W" mintmark which was only available with proof sets, wrapped separately from the proof set in its own United States Mint plastic wrap.
Proposals to eliminate
As of 2024, about a quarter trillion pennies are estimated to be in circulation, or more than 700 pennies for each person the United States.
Proposals to eliminate

Many Americans do not actually spend pennies, but rather only receive them in change at stores and proceed to store them at home, or perhaps return them to a bank for higher denomination currencies, or cash them in at coin counting kiosks.
Proposals to eliminate
Most modern vending machines do not accept pennies, further diminishing their utility.
Proposals to eliminate

In 2001 and 2006, for example, United States Representative Jim Kolbe (R) of Arizona introduced bills which would have stopped production of pennies (in 2001, the Legal Tender Modernization Act, and in 2006, the Currency Overhaul for an Industrious Nation Act).
Proposals to eliminate

Mint, which is a part of the US Department of the Treasury, implemented new regulations on December 14, 2006, which criminalize the melting of pennies and nickels and place limits on export of the coins.
Proposals to eliminate
Violators can be punished with a fine of up to $10,000 USD, imprisoned for a maximum of five years, or both.
Metal content and manufacturing costs
For example, the loss in 2013 was $55 million.

When copper reached a record high in February 2011, the melt value of a 95% copper cent was more than three times its face value.

As of January 21, 2014, a pre-1982 cent contained 2.203 cents' worth of copper and zinc, making it an attractive target for melting by people wanting to sell the metals for profit.

In comparison, post-1982 copper-plated zinc cents have a metallurgical value of only 0.552 cent.

Prior to 1982, the fluctuating price of copper periodically caused penny shortages, as people hoarded them for their perceived metallic value.

Zinc, a major component of U.S. cents minted after mid-1982, is toxic in large quantities.

Swallowing such a coin, which is 97.5% zinc, can cause damage to the stomach lining because of the high solubility of the zinc ion in the acidic stomach.
Toxicity
Coins are the most commonly ingested foreign body in children but generally are allowed to pass spontaneously unless the patient is symptomatic.
Toxicity
Zinc toxicity, mostly in the form of the ingestion of U.S. pennies minted after 1982, is commonly fatal in dogs where it causes a severe hemolytic anemia.

anct_696_umayyad_gold_dinar.title: Gold dinar
sents: lead
The gold dinar (Arabic: ﺩﻳﻨﺎﺭ ذهب) is an Islamic medieval gold coin first issued in AH 77 (696–697 CE) by Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan.
lead
The weight of the dinar is 1 mithqal (4.25 grams or 0.137 troy ounces).
lead
The word dinar comes from the Latin word denarius, which was a silver coin.
lead
The name "dinar" is also used for Sasanid, Kushan, and Kidarite gold coins, though it is not known what the contemporary name was.
lead
The first dinars were issued by the Umayyad Caliphate.
lead
Under the dynasties that followed the use of the dinar spread from Islamic Spain to Central Asia.
Background

Towards the end of the 7th century CE, Arabic copies of solidi – dinars issued by the caliph Abd al-Malik (685–705 CE), who had access to supplies of gold from the upper Nile – began to circulate in areas outside of the Byzantine empire.
Background

These corresponded in weight to only 20 carats (4.0 g) rather than the 24 carats of a recently minted solidus, but matched with the weight of the worn solidi that were circulating in those areas at the time.
First dated coins
The first dated coins that can be assigned to the Muslims are copies of silver Dirhams of the Sassanian ruler Yazdegerd III, struck during the Caliphate of Uthman.
First dated coins

In parallel with the later Khosrau-type Arab-Sassanian coins, first issued under the Well-Guided Caliphs of Islam, a more extensive series was struck with Khosrau's name replaced by that of the local Arab governor or, in two cases, that of the Caliph.
First dated coins
Historical evidence makes it clear that most of these coins bear Hijra dates.
First silver dirham
By the year AH 75 (695 CE) Abd al-Malik had decided on changes to the coinage.
First silver dirham

This experiment, which maintained the Sassanian weight standard of 3.5–4.0 grams was not proceeded with, and in AH 79 (698 CE) a completely new type of silver coin was struck at 14 mints to a new nominal weight of 2.97 grams.
First silver dirham

The average weight of sixty undamaged specimens of AH 79–84 (698–704 CE) is only 2.71 grams, a figure very close to that for a unique coin of (AH 79) 698 struck with no mint name (as was the standard procedure for the gold dinars produced in Damascus).
First silver dirham
These new coins which bore the name of 'dirham', established the style of the Arab-Sassanian predecessors at 25 to 28 mm in diameter.
First silver dirham
On each side there is a three- or four-line legend with a single circular inscription.
First silver dirham
Outside this are three line circles with, at first, five annulets surrounding them.
First silver dirham

The side normally taken as the obverse has as its central legend the Kalima or shahada: "There is no god except God alone, there is no partner with Him." Around it is the mint and date formula reading "In the Name of God: this Dirham was struck in the year ".
First silver dirham
The reverse has a four line central inscription taken from the Surah 112 of the Quran; "Qul hu Allahu Ahad, Allahu-Samad, Lam yalid wa lam yulad wa lam yakul-lahu kufu-an ahad"'.
First silver dirham

The marginal legend states: "Muhammad is the Messenger of God, he was sent with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over every other religion, averse though the idolaters may be" (Quran 9:33).
First gold dinar
The gold coins were first struck to the contemporary standard of 4.4 grams and with one or more Arabic Standing figures on the obverse and an Arabic legend on the reverse.
First gold dinar
Dated coins exist from 680 (AH 74) and are named as 'Dinars'.
First gold dinar

These experimental issues were replaced in 683 (AH 77), except in North Africa and Spain, by completely epigraphical designs very similar to the designs adopted for the silver pieces but with a shorter reverse legend and no annulets or inner circles.
First gold dinar
This weight was reputed to be based on the average of the current Byzantine solidi, was called a Mithqal, a term used earlier for 1 ⁄ 72 of a ratl.
First gold dinar
Two early examples, minted in approximately 692 and 694 C.E., have similar designs.
First gold dinar
In the year 692 C.E., the shahada or profession of faith was added onto the obverse and in 694 C.E. it was added to the reverse.
First gold dinar
In the year 696-7 C.E., images were almost completely removed from coins and were replaced by coins exclusively decorated with inscriptions.
First gold dinar
The issues in gold from North Africa began as copies of the coins of Heraclius and his son (but with abbreviated shahada in Latin), the reverse "cross on steps" losing in most cases its cross piece.
First gold dinar
Later coins are dated by indiction, from Indiction II (703, AH 84–85) changing to the Hijra date in Roman numerals in 713 (AH 94) with Arabic phrases appearing in the field from 716 (AH 97).
First gold dinar
In 684 (AH 100), North Africa came into line with the eastern issues although the mint is named as Ifriqiya.

27 BC – AD 14) tariffed the value of the sestertius as 1 100 {\displaystyle {\tfrac {1}{100}}} of an aureus.

sents: lead
The tetradrachm (Greek: τετράδραχμον, translit. tetrádrachmon) was a large silver coin that originated in Ancient Greece.
lead
It was nominally equivalent to four drachmae.
lead
Over time the tetradrachm effectively became the standard coin of the Antiquity, spreading well beyond the borders of the Greek World.
lead
As a result, tetradrachms were minted in vast quantities by various polities in many weight and fineness standards, though the Athens -derived Attic standard of about 17.2 grams was the most common.
lead
Because of their large size, tetradrachms were often used by various states or rulers to advertise themselves or to deliver political messages.
lead

Popularity of the tetradrachm outlived the political independence of the Greeks and it remained in wide circulation in the Mediterranean up until Crisis of the Third Century, while debased varieties persisted in India and Central Asia into early Middle Ages.
lead
Due to their often high artistic level tetradrachms are eagerly collected in modern times, and well-preserved or rare specimens can reach considerable prices.

525 –510 BC; the abandonment of the "heraldic"-type didrachms and the Archaic tetradrachms (early "owls") of the polis of Athens apparently took place shortly after the Battle of Salamis, 480 BC.

Most well known were the silver mines of Laurium in Athenian countryside.
In Athens

anct_160_marcus_aurelius_denarius.title: Denarius
sents: lead
The denarius (Latin:; pl.: dēnāriī, Latin:) was the standard Roman silver coin from its introduction in the Second Punic War c.
lead
211 BC to the reign of Gordian III (AD 238–244), when it was gradually replaced by the antoninianus.
lead
It continued to be minted in very small quantities, likely for ceremonial purposes, until and through the Tetrarchy (293–313).
lead
The word dēnārius is derived from the Latin dēnī "containing ten", as its value was originally of 10 assēs.
lead
The word for "money" descends from it in Italian (denaro), Slovene (denar), Portuguese (dinheiro), and Spanish (dinero).
lead
Its name also survives in the dinar currency.
lead
Its symbol is represented in Unicode as 𐆖 (U+10196), a numeral monogram that appeared on the obverse in the Republican period, denoting the 10 asses ("X") to 1 denarius ("I") conversion rate.
lead
However it can also be represented as X̶ (capital letter X with combining long stroke overlay).
History
A predecessor of the denarius was first struck in 269 or 268 BC, five years before the First Punic War, with an average weight of 6.81 grams, or 1 ⁄ 48 of a Roman pound.
History
The first distinctively Roman silver coin appeared around 226 BC.
History
This, with a two-horse chariot or biga which was used as a reverse type for some early denarii, was the prototype for the most common designs used on Roman silver coins for a number of years.
History
Rome overhauled its coinage shortly before 211 BC, and introduced the denarius alongside a short-lived denomination called the victoriatus.
History
The denarius contained an average 4.5 grams, or 1 ⁄ 72 of a Roman pound, of silver, and was at first tariffed at ten asses, hence its name, which means 'tenner'.
History
Under the rule of Augustus (27 BC – 14 AD) its weight fell to 3.9 grams (a theoretical weight of 1 ⁄ 84 of a Roman pound).
History
It remained at nearly this weight until the time of Nero (AD 37–68), when it was reduced to 1 ⁄ 96 of a pound, or 3.4 grams.
History
Later Roman emperors also reduced its weight to 3 grams around the late 3rd century.
History
The value at its introduction was 10 asses, giving the denarius its name, which translates as "containing ten".
History
In about 141 BC, it was re-tariffed at 16 asses, to reflect the decrease in weight of the as.
History
The denarius continued to be the main coin of the Roman Empire until it was replaced by the antoninianus in the early 3rd century AD.
History
The coin was last issued, in bronze, under Aurelian between 270 and 275 AD, and in the first years of the reign of Diocletian.
Value, comparisons and silver content
During the republic (509 BC – 27 BC), a legionary earned 112.5 denarii per year (0.3 denarii per day).
Value, comparisons and silver content

Under Julius Caesar, this was doubled to 225 denarii /yr, with soldiers having to pay for their own food and arms, while in the reign of Augustus a Centurion received at least 3,750 denarii per year, and for the highest rank, 15,000 denarii.
Value, comparisons and silver content
27 BC), a common soldier or unskilled laborer would be paid 1 denarius /day (with no tax deductions), around 300% inflation compared to the early period.
Value, comparisons and silver content
Using the cost of bread as a baseline, this pay equates to around US$20 in 2013 terms.
Value, comparisons and silver content
Expressed in terms of the price of silver, and assuming 0.999 purity, a 1 ⁄ 10 troy ounce denarius had a precious metal value of around US$2.60 in 2021.
Value, comparisons and silver content

At the height of the Roman Empire a sextarius (546 ml or about 2 1 ⁄ 4 American cups) of ordinary wine cost roughly one dupondius (1 ⁄ 8 of a denarius); after Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices was issued in 301 AD, the same item cost 8 debased common denarii – 6300% inflation.
Value, comparisons and silver content
Under the Roman Empire (after Nero) the denarius contained approximately 50 grains, 3.24 grams, or 0.105 ozt (about 1 ⁄ 10 troy ounce).
Value, comparisons and silver content
From a purity of greater than 90% silver in the 1st century AD, the denarius fell to under 60% purity by 200 AD, and plummeted to 5% purity by 300 AD.
Influence
In the final years of the 1st century BC Tincomarus, a local ruler in southern Britain, started issuing coins that appear to have been made from melted down denarii.
Influence
The lasting legacy of the denarius can be seen in the use of "d" as the abbreviation for the British penny until 1971.
Influence
The pre-decimal currency of the United Kingdom until 1970 of pounds, shillings and pence was abbreviated as lsd, with "d" referring to denarius and standing for penny.
Use in the Bible
In the New Testament, the gospels refer to the denarius as a day's wage for a common laborer (Matthew 20:2, John 12:5).
Use in the Bible
Thus, in the conditions pictured by Revelation 6, the normal income for a working-class family would buy enough food for only one person.
Use in the Bible
The denarius is also mentioned in the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant & in Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37).
Use in the Bible
The Render unto Caesar passage in Matthew 22:15–22 and Mark 12:13–17 uses the word (δηνάριον) to describe the coin held up by Jesus, translated in the King James Bible as " tribute penny ".

At the height of the Roman Empire a sextarius (546 ml or about 2 1 ⁄ 4 American cups) of ordinary wine cost roughly one dupondius (1 ⁄ 8 of a denarius); after Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices was issued in 301 AD, the same item cost 8 debased common denarii – 6300% inflation.
Value, comparisons and silver content
Under the Roman Empire (after Nero) the denarius contained approximately 50 grains, 3.24 grams, or 0.105 ozt (about 1 ⁄ 10 troy ounce).
Value, comparisons and silver content
From a purity of greater than 90% silver in the 1st century AD, the denarius fell to under 60% purity by 200 AD, and plummeted to 5% purity by 300 AD.
Influence
In the final years of the 1st century BC Tincomarus, a local ruler in southern Britain, started issuing coins that appear to have been made from melted down denarii.
Influence
The lasting legacy of the denarius can be seen in the use of "d" as the abbreviation for the British penny until 1971.
Influence
The pre-decimal currency of the United Kingdom until 1970 of pounds, shillings and pence was abbreviated as lsd, with "d" referring to denarius and standing for penny.
Use in the Bible
In the New Testament, the gospels refer to the denarius as a day's wage for a common laborer (Matthew 20:2, John 12:5).
Use in the Bible
Thus, in the conditions pictured by Revelation 6, the normal income for a working-class family would buy enough food for only one person.
Use in the Bible
The denarius is also mentioned in the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant & in Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37).
Use in the Bible
The Render unto Caesar passage in Matthew 22:15–22 and Mark 12:13–17 uses the word (δηνάριον) to describe the coin held up by Jesus, translated in the King James Bible as " tribute penny ".

History

When the Lincoln one-cent coin made its initial appearance in 1909, it marked a radical departure from the accepted styling of United States coinage, as it was the first regular coin to bear a portrait other than the mythical Liberty which appeared on most pre-1909 regular coins.
History
Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th U.S. president, thought American coins were so common and uninspiring that he attempted to get the motto "In God We Trust" removed as offending religion.
History

Roosevelt, who considered Lincoln the savior of the Union and the greatest Republican president, and who also considered himself Lincoln's political heir, ordered the new Lincoln cent to be based on Brenner's work and to be released just in time to commemorate Lincoln's 100th birthday in 1909.

History
Franklin MacVeagh gave his approval on July 14, 1909, and not quite three weeks later, on August 2, the new coin was released to the public.
History
In 1918, after the controversy over Brenner's name and initials on the reverse had died down, his initials were placed on the obverse with no further controversy.

Thus in 1909 the U.S. had six different cents: the 1909 and 1909-S Indian Head cents, and four Lincoln coins: 1909 VDB, 1909-S VDB, 1909 and 1909-S.

Proposals to eliminate
As of 2024, about a quarter trillion pennies are estimated to be in circulation, or more than 700 pennies for each person the United States.
Proposals to eliminate

Many Americans do not actually spend pennies, but rather only receive them in change at stores and proceed to store them at home, or perhaps return them to a bank for higher denomination currencies, or cash them in at coin counting kiosks.
Proposals to eliminate
Most modern vending machines do not accept pennies, further diminishing their utility.
Proposals to eliminate

In 2001 and 2006, for example, United States Representative Jim Kolbe (R) of Arizona introduced bills which would have stopped production of pennies (in 2001, the Legal Tender Modernization Act, and in 2006, the Currency Overhaul for an Industrious Nation Act).
Proposals to eliminate

Mint, which is a part of the US Department of the Treasury, implemented new regulations on December 14, 2006, which criminalize the melting of pennies and nickels and place limits on export of the coins.
Proposals to eliminate
Violators can be punished with a fine of up to $10,000 USD, imprisoned for a maximum of five years, or both.
Metal content and manufacturing costs
For example, the loss in 2013 was $55 million.
Metal content and manufacturing costs
When copper reached a record high in February 2011, the melt value of a 95% copper cent was more than three times its face value.
Metal content and manufacturing costs
As of January 21, 2014, a pre-1982 cent contained 2.203 cents' worth of copper and zinc, making it an attractive target for melting by people wanting to sell the metals for profit.
Metal content and manufacturing costs
In comparison, post-1982 copper-plated zinc cents have a metallurgical value of only 0.552 cent.
Metal content and manufacturing costs
Prior to 1982, the fluctuating price of copper periodically caused penny shortages, as people hoarded them for their perceived metallic value.
Toxicity
Zinc, a major component of U.S. cents minted after mid-1982, is toxic in large quantities.
Toxicity
Swallowing such a coin, which is 97.5% zinc, can cause damage to the stomach lining because of the high solubility of the zinc ion in the acidic stomach.
Toxicity
Coins are the most commonly ingested foreign body in children but generally are allowed to pass spontaneously unless the patient is symptomatic.
Toxicity
Zinc toxicity, mostly in the form of the ingestion of U.S. pennies minted after 1982, is commonly fatal in dogs where it causes a severe hemolytic anemia.

anct_1489_henry_vii_sovereign.title: Sovereign (British coin)

Edge: Milled (some not intended for circulation have plain edge)
Mint marks: Various. Found on reverse on exergue between design and date for Saint George and the Dragon sovereigns, and under the wreath for shield back sovereigns, or below bust on obverse on earlier Australian issues.
Design: The British monarch currently depicted on the coinage (Elizabeth II depicted here)

sents: lead
The sovereign is a British gold coin with a nominal value of one pound sterling (£1) and contains 0.2354 troy oz of pure gold.
lead
Struck since 1817, it was originally a circulating coin that was accepted in Britain and elsewhere in the world; it is now a bullion coin and is sometimes mounted in jewellery.
lead
In addition, circulation strikes and proof examples are often collected for their numismatic value.
lead
In most recent years, it has borne the design of Saint George and the Dragon on the reverse; the initials (B P) of the designer, Benedetto Pistrucci, are visible to the right of the date.
lead
The coin was named after the English gold sovereign, which was last minted about 1603, and originated as part of the Great Recoinage of 1816.
lead
Many in Parliament believed a one-pound coin should be issued rather than the 21-shilling guinea that was struck until that time.
lead
The Master of the Mint, William Wellesley Pole had Pistrucci design the new coin; his depiction was also used for other gold coins.
lead
Originally, the coin was unpopular because the public preferred the convenience of banknotes but paper currency of value £1 was soon limited by law.
Background and authorisation
There had been an English coin known as the sovereign, first authorised by Henry VII in 1489.
Background and authorisation
It had a diameter of 42 millimetres (1.7 in), and weighed 15.55 grams (0.500 troy ounces), twice the weight of the existing gold coin, the ryal.
Background and authorisation
The new coin was struck in response to a large influx of gold into Europe from West Africa in the 1480s, and Henry at first called it the double ryal, but soon changed the name to sovereign.
Background and authorisation
The English sovereign, the country's first coin to be valued at one pound, was struck by the monarchs of the 16th century, the size and fineness often being altered.
Background and authorisation
In the 1660s, following the Restoration of Charles II and the mechanisation of the Royal Mint that quickly followed, a new twenty-shilling gold coin was issued.
Background and authorisation
It had no special name at first but the public soon nicknamed it the guinea and this became the accepted term.
Background and authorisation
Thus, it came to trade at 21 shillings or even sixpence more.
Background and authorisation
Popular in commerce, the coin's value was set by the government at 21 shillings in silver in 1717, and was subject to revision downwards, though in practice this did not occur.
Background and authorisation
The term sovereign, referring to a coin, fell from use—it does not appear in Samuel Johnson's dictionary, compiled in the 1750s.
Background and authorisation
After the war, Parliament, by the Coinage Act 1816, placed Britain officially on the gold standard, with the pound to be defined as a given quantity of gold.
Background and authorisation
A committee of the Privy Council recommended gold coins of ten shillings, twenty shillings, two pounds and five pounds be issued, and this was accepted by George, Prince Regent on 3 August 1816.
Creation
William Wellesley Pole, elder brother of the Duke of Wellington, was appointed Master of the Mint (at that time a junior government position) in 1812, with a mandate to reform the Royal Mint.
Creation
Formal instruction to the Mint came with an indenture dated February 1817, directing the Royal Mint to strike gold sovereigns.
Creation
The Italian sculptor Benedetto Pistrucci came to London early in 1816.
Creation
In 1816, Pole hired Pistrucci to create models for the new coinage.
Creation
After completing Lady Spencer's commission, by most accounts, Pistrucci suggested to Pole that an appropriate subject for the sovereign would be Saint George.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
The original 1817 design had the saintly knight still carrying part of his broken spear.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
This was changed to a sword when the garter that originally surrounded the design was eliminated in 1821, and George is intended to have broken his spear earlier in the encounter with the dragon.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design
Also removed in 1821 was the plume of hair, or streamer, behind George's helmet; it was restored in 1887, modified in 1893 and 1902, and eliminated in 2009.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design

When Pistrucci created the coin, Neoclassicism was all the rage in London, and he may have been inspired by the Elgin Marbles, which were exhibited from 1807, and which he probably saw soon after his arrival in London.
Pistrucci's George and Dragon design

Pistrucci's sovereign was unusual for a British coin of the 19th century in not having a heraldic design, but this was consistent with Pole's desire to make the sovereign look as different from the guinea as possible.
Early years (1817–1837)
When the sovereign entered circulation in late 1817, it was not initially popular, as the public preferred the convenience of the banknotes the sovereign had been intended to replace.
Early years (1817–1837)
Lack of demand meant that mintages dropped from 2,347,230 in 1818 to 3,574 the following year.
Early years (1817–1837)

Another reason why few sovereigns were struck in 1819 was a proposal, eventually rejected, by economist David Ricardo to eliminate gold as a coinage metal, though making it available on demand from the Bank of England.
Early years (1817–1837)
Once this plan was abandoned in 1820, the Bank encouraged the circulation of gold sovereigns, but acceptance among the British public was slow.
Early years (1817–1837)

The early sovereigns were heavily exported; in 1819, Robert Peel estimated that of the some £5,000,000 in gold struck in France since the previous year, three-quarters of the gold used had come from the new British coinage, melted down.
Early years (1817–1837)

Many more sovereigns were exported to France in the 1820s as the metal alloyed with the gold included silver, which could be profitably recovered, with the gold often returned to Britain and struck again into sovereigns.
Early years (1817–1837)
Beginning in 1829, the Mint was able to eliminate the silver, but the drain on sovereigns from before then continued.
Early years (1817–1837)
George III died in January 1820, succeeded by George, Prince Regent, as George IV.
Early years (1817–1837)
The new version was authorised by an Order in Council of 5 May 1821.
Early years (1817–1837)
Pistrucci refused to copy the work of another artist and was barred from further work on the coinage.
Early years (1817–1837)
Second Engraver (later Chief Engraver) William Wyon was assigned to translate Chantrey's bust into a coin design, and the new sovereign came into use during 1825.
Early years (1817–1837)
The George and Dragon design would not again appear on the sovereign until 1871.
Early years (1817–1837)
William IV 's accession in 1830 upon the death of his brother George IV led to new designs for the sovereign, with the new king's depiction engraved by William Wyon based on a bust by Chantrey.
Victorian era
The new coin was approved on 26 February 1838, and with the exception of 1840 and 1867, the "shield back" sovereign was struck at the Royal Mint in London every year from 1838 to 1874.
Victorian era
Sovereigns struck in London with the shield design between 1863 and 1874 bear small numbers under the shield, representing which coinage die was used.
Victorian era

By 1850, some £94 million in sovereigns and half sovereigns had been struck and circulated widely, well beyond Britain's shores, a dispersion aided by the British government, who saw the sovereign's use as an auxiliary to their imperialist ambitions.
Victorian era

In 1838, when the legacy of James Smithson was converted into gold in preparation for transmission to the United States, American authorities requested recently-struck sovereigns, likely to maximise the quantity of gold when the sovereigns were melted after arrival in the United States.
Victorian era
The weight of a newly-struck sovereign was intended to be 123.274 grains (7.98805 g).
Victorian era
It ceased to be legal currency for £1 if found to weigh less than 122 1 ⁄ 2 grains (i.e. a deficiency of 1 1 ⁄ 2 pence in gold per sovereign).
Victorian era
Between 1842 and 1845, the Bank withdrew and had recoined some £14 million in lightweight gold, about one-third the amount of that metal in circulation.
Victorian era
This not only kept the sovereign to standard, it probably removed most of the remaining guineas still in commerce.
Victorian era

The unlucky holder of a lightweight gold coin could only turn it in as bullion, would lose at least 1 1 ⁄ 2 pence because of the lightness and often had to pay an equal amount to cover the Bank of England's costs.
Victorian era

The California Gold Rush and other discoveries of the 1840s and 1850s boosted the amount of available gold and also the number of sovereigns struck, with £150 million in sovereigns and half sovereigns coined between 1850 and 1875.
Victorian era

The Coinage Act 1889 also authorised the Bank of England to redeem worn gold coins from before Victoria's reign, but on 22 November 1890 all gold coins from before her reign were called in by Royal Proclamation and demonetised effective 28 February 1891.
Victorian era
The sovereign was seen in fiction: in Dickens ' Oliver Twist, Mrs Bumble is paid £25 in sovereigns for her information.
Victorian era

Although many sovereigns were melted down for recoining on reaching a foreign land (as were those for the Smithsonian) it was regarded as a circulating coin in dozens of British colonies and even in nations such as Brazil and Portugal; the latter accepted it at a value of 4,500 reis.
Victorian era
The return of Saint George was approved by the Queen, and authorised by an Order in Council dated 14 January 1871.
Victorian era
The two designs were struck side by side in London from 1871 to 1874, and at the Australian branch mints until 1887, after which the Pistrucci design alone was used.
Victorian era

Victorian era
Wyon's "Young head" of Queen Victoria for the sovereign's obverse was struck from 1838 until 1887, when it was replaced by the " Jubilee head " by Joseph Boehm.
Victorian era

Melbourne and Perth stopped striking sovereigns after 1931, with Sydney having closed in 1926.

The 1932 sovereigns struck at Pretoria were the last to be issued intended as currency at their face value.

Churchill's successor, George Goschen, urged issuing banknotes to replace the gold coins, saying he preferred £20 million in gold in the Bank of England to thirty million sovereigns in the hands of the public.

After the war, the sovereign did not return to commerce in Britain, with the pieces usually worth more as gold than as currency.

In 1925, the Chancellor, Winston Churchill, secured the passage of the Gold Standard Act 1925, restoring Britain to that standard, but with gold to be kept in reserve rather than as a means of circulation.

The effort failed—Churchill regarded it as the worst mistake of his life—but some lightweight sovereigns were melted and restruck dated 1925, and were released only later.

Sovereigns were struck in 1953, the coronation year of Elizabeth II, bearing the portrait of her by Mary Gillick, though the gold pieces were placed only in the major museums.

The sovereign's role in popular culture continued: in the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Q issues James Bond with a briefcase, the handle of which contains 50 sovereigns.

The last of the Gillick sovereigns had been struck in 1968; when production resumed in 1974, it was with a portrait by Arnold Machin.

The last coin minted at Tower Hill, in 1975, was a sovereign.

The reverse of the 1489 piece depicts a double Tudor rose fronted by the royal arms; a similar design with updated arms graces the reverse of the 1989 sovereign.

lead

lead
The derivatives of the noble, the half noble and quarter noble, on the other hand, were produced in quantity and were very popular.
lead
The value of the coin was six shillings and eight pence (written 6/8, or 6s.8d., vjs.viijd.), which was equivalent to eighty old pence or one-third of a pound sterling.

sents: lead
The angel was an English gold coin introduced by Edward IV in 1465.
lead
It was patterned after the French angelot or ange, which had been issued since 1340.
lead
The name derived from its representation of the archangel Michael slaying a dragon.
lead
As it was considered a new issue of the noble, it was also called the angel-noble.
lead
In 1472, the half-angel was introduced with a similar design weighing 40 grains (2.6 grammes) with a diameter of 20 to 21 millimetres.
Value
The angel varied in value from 6 shillings 8 pence to 11 shillings between Edward's reign and the time of James I.
Value
In 1526 during the reign of Henry VIII, it increased to seven shillings and six pence (7/6) or 90 pence.
Value
In 1544, it increased again to eight shillings (8/-) or 96 pence.
Value
In 1550 during the reign of Edward VI it increased to ten shillings (10/-) or 120 pence or £ 1 ⁄ 2.
Value
In 1612 during the reign of James I it increased to eleven shillings (11/-) or 132 pence.
Value
In 1619 it decreased to ten shillings (10/-) and at that point in time it weighed 70 grains (4.5 g).
Value
It was last minted during the reign of Charles I in 1642 before the English Civil War (1642–1651).
Value
In 1663, Charles II replaced the existing coinage with entirely new designs struck by machine ("milled").

After his execution in 1649, royalists believed that Angel coins that had been given to sufferers by the "martyred" King Charles I could miraculously cure scrofula.

In 1660, Charles II began handing out gold-plated "touch-pieces" in the place of Angel coins.

(The Jacobite touch pieces were plated in silver instead of gold as an economy measure.) They were last issued by the fourth and final direct Jacobite pretender, "Henry IX" Stuart (the Cardinal King) until his death in 1807.

The angel was such an iconic coin that many English pubs were named after it.
Social impact
The 1610 General Assembly of the Church of Scotland in Glasgow was named after the coins.

lead

It has been the lowest face-value physical unit of U.S. currency since the abolition of the half-cent in 1857 (the abstract mill, which has never been minted, equal to a tenth of a cent, continues to see limited use in the fields of taxation and finance).
lead
The first U.S. cent was produced in 1787, and the cent has been issued primarily as a copper or copper-plated coin throughout its history.
lead
Due to inflation, pennies have lost virtually all their purchasing power and are often viewed as an expensive burden to businesses, banks, government (especially mints) and the public in general.
lead
The penny is issued in its current form as the Lincoln cent, with its obverse featuring the profile of President Abraham Lincoln since 1909, the centennial of his birth.
lead
From 1959 (the sesquicentennial of Lincoln's birth) to 2008, the reverse featured the Lincoln Memorial.
lead
Four different reverse designs in 2009 honored Lincoln's 200th birthday and a new, "permanent" reverse – the Union Shield – was introduced in 2010.

During the early 1970s, the price of copper rose to the point where the cent contained almost one cent's worth of copper.

Designs

When the Lincoln one-cent coin made its initial appearance in 1909, it marked a radical departure from the accepted styling of United States coinage, as it was the first regular coin to bear a portrait other than the mythical Liberty which appeared on most pre-1909 regular coins.

Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th U.S. president, thought American coins were so common and uninspiring that he attempted to get the motto "In God We Trust" removed as offending religion.
History

Proposals to eliminate
As of 2024, about a quarter trillion pennies are estimated to be in circulation, or more than 700 pennies for each person the United States.
Proposals to eliminate

Many Americans do not actually spend pennies, but rather only receive them in change at stores and proceed to store them at home, or perhaps return them to a bank for higher denomination currencies, or cash them in at coin counting kiosks.
Proposals to eliminate
Most modern vending machines do not accept pennies, further diminishing their utility.
Proposals to eliminate

In 2001 and 2006, for example, United States Representative Jim Kolbe (R) of Arizona introduced bills which would have stopped production of pennies (in 2001, the Legal Tender Modernization Act, and in 2006, the Currency Overhaul for an Industrious Nation Act).

Toxicity

The Spanish dollar, also known as the piece of eight (Spanish: real de a ocho, dólar, peso duro, peso fuerte or peso), is a silver coin of approximately 38 mm (1.5 in) diameter worth eight Spanish reales.
lead
It was minted in the Spanish Empire following a monetary reform in 1497 with content 25.563 g (0.8219 ozt) fine silver.
lead
It was widely used as the first international currency because of its uniformity in standard and milling characteristics.
lead
Some countries countermarked the Spanish dollar so it could be used as their local currency.
lead
Because the Spanish dollar was widely used in Europe, the Americas, and the Far East, it became the first world currency by the 16th century.
lead

The Spanish dollar was the coin upon which the original United States dollar was based (at 0.7735 troy ounces or 24.06 grams), and it remained legal tender in the United States until the Coinage Act of 1857.
lead
Many other currencies around the world, such as the Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan, were initially based on the Spanish dollar and other 8-real coins.
lead
Most theories trace the origin of the "$" symbol, which originally had two vertical bars, to the pillars of Hercules wrapped in ribbons that appear on the reverse side of the Spanish dollar.
Etymology
In the 16th century, Count Hieronymus Schlick of Bohemia began minting a silver coin known as a Joachimsthaler, named after Joachimsthal, the valley in the Ore Mountains where the silver was mined.
Europe and colonial North America
The Joachimsthaler weighed 451 Troy grains (29.2 g; 0.94 ozt) of silver.
Europe and colonial North America

The Netherlands also introduced its own dollars in the 16th century: the Burgundian Cross Thaler (Bourgondrische Kruisdaalder), the German-inspired Rijksdaalder, and the Dutch lion dollar (leeuwendaalder).
Europe and colonial North America
For the English North American colonists, however, the Spanish peso or "piece of eight" has always held first place, and this coin was also called the "dollar" as early as 1581.
Spain

After the introduction of the Guldengroschen in Austria in 1486, the concept of a large silver coin with high purity (sometimes known as "specie" coinage) eventually spread throughout the rest of Europe.
Spain
This was supplemented in 1537 by the gold escudo, minted at 68 to a mark of gold 0.917 fine (fineness reduced to 0.906 in 1742 and 0.875 in 1786).
Spain
It was valued at 15–16 reales or approximately 2 dollars.
Spain
The famed Gold Doubloon was worth 2 escudos or approximately 4 dollars.
Spain
From the 15th to the 19th centuries the coin was minted with several different designs at various mints in Spain and the New World, having gained wide acceptance beyond Spain's borders.
Spain
The dollar or peso was divided into 8 reales in Spanish Latin America until the 19th century when the peso was divided into 100 centavos.
Spain
Spain's adoption of the peseta in 1869 and its joining the Latin Monetary Union meant the effective end of the last vestiges of the Spanish dollar in Spain itself.
Spain
However, the 5-peseta coin (or duro) was slightly smaller and lighter but was also of high purity (90%) silver.
Spain
In the 1990s, commemorative 2,000-peseta coins were minted, similar in size and weight to the dollar.
Mexico
Following independence in 1821, Mexican coinage of silver reales and gold escudos followed that of Spanish lines until decimalization and the introduction of the peso worth 8 reales or 100 centavos.
Mexico

It continued to be minted to Spanish standards throughout the 19th century, with the peso at 27.07 grams (0.955 oz) of 0.9028 fine silver, and the escudo at 3.383 grams (0.1193 oz) of 0.875 fine gold.
Mexico
The Mexican peso or 8-real coin continued to be a popular international trading coin throughout the 19th century.
Mexico
After 1918, the peso was reduced in size and fineness, with further reductions in the 1940s and 1950s.
Mexico
However, 2- (1921), 5- (1947) and 10-peso (1955) coins were minted during the same period with sizes and fineness similar to the old peso.
Australia

After the colony of New South Wales was founded in Australia in 1788, it ran into the problem of a lack of coinage, particularly since trading vessels took coins out of the colony in exchange for their cargo.
Australia
In 1813, Governor Lachlan Macquarie made creative use of £10,000 in Spanish dollars sent by the British government.
Australia
The punched centre, known as the "dump", was valued at 15 pence, and the outer rim, known as the " holey dollar ", was worth five shillings.
Australia
The obverse of the holey dollar was stamped the words "New South Wales" and the date, 1813, and the reverse with the words "five shillings".
Australia
The obverse of the dump was stamped with a crown, the words "New South Wales" and the date, 1813, and the reverse with the words "fifteen pence".
Australia
The mutilated coins became the first official currency produced specifically for circulation in Australia.
Australia

The British Parliament passed the Sterling Silver Money Act in 1825, which made British coins the only recognised form of currency and ended any legitimate use of the holey dollar and dump in the Australian colonies.
United States
By far the leading specie coin circulating in America was the Spanish silver dollar, defined as consisting of 387 grains of pure silver.
United States
The Spanish silver dollar had been the world's outstanding coin since the early 16th century, and was spread partially by dint of the vast silver output of the Spanish colonies in Latin America.
United States
More important, however, was that the Spanish dollar, from the 16th to the 19th century, was relatively the most stable and least debased coin in the Western world.
United States
The Coinage Act of 1792 specified that the U.S. dollar would contain 371.25 grains (24.057 g) pure or 416 grains (26.96 g) standard silver.
United States
Initially this dollar was comparable to the 371–373 grains found in circulating Spanish dollars and aided in its exportation overseas.
United States
The restoration of the old 0.9028 fineness in the Mexican peso after 1821, however, increased the latter's silver content to 24.44 g and reduced the export demand for U.S. dollars.
United States
Spanish coinage was legal tender in the United States until the Coinage Act of 1857 discontinued the practice.
United States

The pricing of equities on U.S. stock exchanges in 1 ⁄ 8 -dollar denominations persisted until the New York Stock Exchange converted first to pricing in sixteenths of a dollar on 24 June 1997, and then in 2001 to decimal pricing.
Asia
The first Chinese yuan coins had the same specification as a Spanish dollar, leading to a continuing equivalence in some respects between the names "yuan" and "dollar" in the Chinese language.
Fiction
In modern pop culture and fiction, pieces of eight are most often associated with the popular notion of pirates.
Fiction

In the film Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End the Pirate Lords must meet together by presenting the "Nine Pieces of Eight", since these Pieces were used to seal the goddess Calypso in her human form by the first Brethren Court.
Fiction
Pieces of Eight is the eighth studio album and second concept album by Styx, released on 1 September 1978.

anct_117_trajan_sestertius.title: Sestertius
sents: lead
The sestertius (pl.: sestertii) or sesterce (pl.: sesterces) was an ancient Roman coin.
lead
During the Roman Republic it was a small, silver coin issued only on rare occasions.
lead
During the Roman Empire it was a large brass coin.
lead

The name sestertius means "two and one half", referring to its nominal value of two and a half asses (a bronze Roman coin, singular as), a value that was useful for commerce because it was one quarter of a denarius, a coin worth ten asses.
lead
The name is derived from semis, "half" and tertius, "third", in which "third" refers to the third as: the sestertius was worth two full asses and half of a third.
lead

English-language sources routinely use the original Latin form sestertius, plural sestertii; but older literature frequently uses sesterce, plural sesterces, terce being the English equivalent of tertius.
History
211 BC as a small silver coin valued at one-quarter of a denarius (and thus one hundredth of an aureus).
History
A silver denarius was supposed to weigh about 4.5 grams, valued at ten asses, with the silver sestertius valued at two and a half asses (1.125 grammes).
History
In or about 23 BC, with the coinage reform of Augustus, the sestertius was reintroduced as a large brass denomination, while the as, now made of copper, was worth one quarter of a sestertius.
History
The sestertius was produced as the largest brass denomination until the late 3rd century AD.
History
Most were struck in the mint of Rome but from AD 64 during the reign of Nero (AD 54–68) and Vespasian (AD 69–79), the mint of Lyon (Lugdunum), supplemented production.
History
The brass sestertius typically weighs in the region of 25 to 28 grams, is around 32–34 mm in diameter and about 4 mm thick.
History
Sestertii continued to be struck until the late 3rd century, although there was a marked deterioration in the quality of the metal used and the striking even though portraiture remained strong.
History

Later emperors increasingly relied on melting down older sestertii, a process which led to the zinc component being gradually lost as it burned off in the high temperatures needed to melt copper (zinc melts at 419 °C but boils at 907 °C, copper melts at 1085 °C).
History
In the 1st century AD, everyday small change was dominated by the dupondius and as, but in the 2nd century, as inflation hit, the sestertius became the dominant small change.
History
In the 3rd century silver coinage contained less and less silver, and more and more copper or bronze.
History
By the 260s and 270s the main unit was the double-denarius, the Antoninianus, but by then these small coins were almost all bronze.
History
Although these coins were theoretically worth eight sestertii, the average sestertius was worth far more in plain terms of the metal it contained.
History
Some of the last sestertii were struck by Aurelian (270–275 AD).
History
In the coinage reforms of the 4th century, the sestertius played no part and passed into history.
Unit of account
The wealthy general and politician of the late Roman Republic, Crassus, who fought in the war to defeat Spartacus, was said by Pliny the Elder to have had "estates worth 200 million sesterces".
Unit of account
0.5 L) of wine anywhere from less than half to more than one sestertius.
Unit of account
One modius (6.67 kg) of wheat in 79 AD Pompeii cost seven sestertii, of rye three sestertii, a bucket two sestertii, a tunic fifteen sestertii, a donkey five hundred sestertii.
Unit of account

According to Tacitus ' Annals, book I, chapter 17.4 and 17.5, soldiers of the Rhine army who rose against Tiberius were paid ten asses a day, out of which they had to pay, among other things, for their own uniforms.
Unit of account
Records from Pompeii show a slave being sold at auction for 6,252 sestertii.
Unit of account
75 –125 AD, records the sale of a Gallic slave girl called Fortunata for 600 denarii, equal to 2,400 sestertii, to a man called Vegetus.
Unit of account

It is difficult to make any comparisons with modern coinage or prices, but for most of the 1st century AD, the ordinary legionary was paid nine hundred sestertii per annum, rising to twelve hundred under Domitian (81–96 AD), the equivalent of 3.3 sestertii per day.
Unit of account
Half of it was deducted for living costs, leaving the soldier, if he was lucky enough to get paid, with about 1.65 sestertii per day.
Numismatic value
The most celebrated are those produced for Nero (54–68 AD) between the years 64 and 68 AD, created by some of the most accomplished coin engravers in history.
Numismatic value

The series issued by Hadrian (117–138 AD), recording his travels around the Roman Empire, depicts the Empire at its height, and included the first representation on a coin of the figure of Britannia; centuries later it was revived by English king Charles II, and continues to feature on the United Kingdom coinage.
Numismatic value
As a result of ceasing production and withdrawals from circulation in the 4th century, sestertii are less common as a whole compared to other Roman bronze coins.
Numismatic value
Fully struck examples with sharp detail often command high premiums at auction.

anct_250_bc_seleucid_tetradrachm.title: Tetradrachm
sents: lead
The tetradrachm (Greek: τετράδραχμον, translit. tetrádrachmon) was a large silver coin that originated in Ancient Greece.
lead
It was nominally equivalent to four drachmae.
lead
Over time the tetradrachm effectively became the standard coin of the Antiquity, spreading well beyond the borders of the Greek World.
lead
As a result, tetradrachms were minted in vast quantities by various polities in many weight and fineness standards, though the Athens -derived Attic standard of about 17.2 grams was the most common.
lead
Because of their large size, tetradrachms were often used by various states or rulers to advertise themselves or to deliver political messages.
lead

Popularity of the tetradrachm outlived the political independence of the Greeks and it remained in wide circulation in the Mediterranean up until Crisis of the Third Century, while debased varieties persisted in India and Central Asia into early Middle Ages.
lead
Due to their often high artistic level tetradrachms are eagerly collected in modern times, and well-preserved or rare specimens can reach considerable prices.
In Athens
525 –510 BC; the abandonment of the "heraldic"-type didrachms and the Archaic tetradrachms (early "owls") of the polis of Athens apparently took place shortly after the Battle of Salamis, 480 BC.
In Athens
Most well known were the silver mines of Laurium in Athenian countryside.
In Athens
To differentiate their currency from the rival coinage of Aegina using the Aeginetic stater of about 12.3 grams, Athens minted its tetradrachm based on the "Attic" standard of 4.3 grams per drachma.

anct_1600_elizabeth_i_sixpence.title: Sixpence (British coin)

Design: Profile of the monarch (Elizabeth II design shown)

sents: lead
The British sixpence (/ ˈ s ɪ k s p ən s /) piece, sometimes known as a tanner or sixpenny bit, was a denomination of sterling coinage worth 1 ⁄ 40 of one pound or half of one shilling.
lead
It was first minted in 1551, during the reign of Edward VI, and circulated until 1980.
lead
The coin was made from silver from its introduction in 1551 until 1947, and thereafter in cupronickel.
lead

Before Decimal Day in 1971, sterling used the Carolingian monetary system (£sd), under which the largest unit was a pound (£), divisible into 20 shillings (s), each worth 12 pence (d), the value of two pre-decimal sixpence coins.
lead
Following decimalisation, the old sixpence had a value of 2 + 1 ⁄ 2 new pence (£0.025).
lead

In 2016, new decimal sixpences (face value £0.06) began being minted by the Royal Mint as commemorative issues; these coins have been produced for each year since then, and are minted in sterling silver.
lead
They are not intended for circulation as tender, but just like older mintages, these coins continue to have uses in especially Christmas and wedding traditions; cf. § Cultural significance, below.
History
The first sixpences were minted in 1551, during the reign of Edward VI.
History
They came about as a result of the debasement of silver coinage in the 1540s, in particular the silver testoon, which fell in value from 12d to 6d.
History
The Royal Mint undertook a massive recoinage programme in 1816, with large quantities of gold and silver coin being minted.
History
Previous issues of silver coinage had been irregular, and the previous issue, minted in 1787, had done little to alleviate the chronic shortage of silver coinage in general circulation.
History
New silver coinage was to be of.925 (sterling) standard, with silver coins to be minted at 66 shillings to the pound weight.
History
Hence, newly minted sixpences weighed 1 ⁄ 11 troy ounce, equivalent to 43.636 grains or 2.828 grams.
History
The Royal Mint debased the silver coinage in 1920 from 92.5% silver to 50% silver.
History
The minting of silver coinage of the pound sterling ceased completely in 1946 for similar reasons, exacerbated by the costs of the Second World War.
History
Beginning with Lord Wrottesley 's proposals in the 1820s, there were various attempts to decimalise the pound sterling over the next century and a half.
History
The decision to decimalise was announced in 1966, with the pound to be divided into 100, rather than 240, pence.
History
Decimal Day was set as 15 February 1971, and a whole range of new coins were introduced.
History
Sixpences continued to be legal tender, with a value of 2 + 1 ⁄ 2 new pence, until 30 June 1980.
2016 decimal sixpence
In 2016, the Royal Mint began minting legal tender decimal sixpence coins in silver, intended to be bought as Christmas presents.
2016 decimal sixpence
These coins are heavier than the pre-1970 sixpence (3.35 grams instead of 2.83 grams), and have a denomination of six new pence (6p) instead of six old pence (6d).
Design

Unusually, the sixpences minted in 1561 and 1562 were milled, i.e. produced by machine rather than by hand, with the press of the Frenchman Eloy Mestrelle, who had been granted authority to mint coins by the queen.
Design
Although of higher quality than hammered coins, Mestrelle's sixpences were more expensive to produce, and machine-struck coinage ceased to be minted in 1572.
Design

Charles I sixpences follow the usual design, except that coins minted after 1630 do not bear a date, and the reverse inscription reads CHRISTO AVSPICE REGNO, meaning " I reign under the auspices of Christ ".
Design
In 1656 the minting of milled coinage resumed, this time with the press of the Frenchman Peter Blondeau.
Design
With the exception of a withdrawn 1887 issue, Victoria and Edward VII sixpences share this reverse.
Design
The reverse of the 1887 issue is broadly the same as the post-1816 George III coins.
Design
The government agreed to remove the coin from circulation in November 1887 and change the reverse.
Design

The reverse of George V sixpences minted prior to 1926 feature an alternative reverse design composed of a crown surmounted by a lion, with those minted after 1926 featuring a design of six oak sprigs divided by six acorns.
Design
Only a handful of Edward VIII sixpences were ever minted, and none of these entered circulation.
Design
The final change in the design of the sixpence came in 1953 when a new reverse was designed for the sixpences of Elizabeth II.
Cultural significance
Prepared on Stir-up Sunday, the last Sunday before the start of Advent, the coin would be placed into the mixture, then the mixture was stirred by every member of the family.
Cultural significance

In Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream (Act 4, Scene 2), we learn that by his absence (ensorcelled in Titania's bower) Bottom the Weaver will forgo sixpence a day for life from Theseus the Duke of Athens.
Cultural significance
Somerset Maugham 's 1919 novel, The Moon and Sixpence, and appears in both the title and as a plot device in Michael Paraskos 's novel In Search of Sixpence.
Cultural significance
The sixpence appears in the English nursery rhyme " Sing a Song of Sixpence " published in London in 1744.
Cultural significance
Half a Sixpence is the title of the 1963 West End stage musical, and the subsequent 1967 musical film version, of H.
Cultural significance

An elaborated version was published in 1941, words and music by Elton Box & Desmond Cox. the singer tells the tale of spending twopence (per verse) until he has "no-pence to send home to my wife – poor wife."
Cultural significance
Sixpence None the Richer (also known as Sixpence) is an American rock band whose name was inspired by a passage from the book Mere Christianity by C.
Cultural significance
Penguin Books initially sold books in the 1930s through Woolworths and other high street stores for sixpence.

anct_1820_chinese_cash_coin.title: Cash (Chinese coin)
sents: lead

The cash or qian was a type of coin of China and the Sinosphere, used from the 4th century BC until the 20th century AD, characterised by their round outer shape and a square center hole (Chinese: 方穿; pinyin: fāng chuān; Jyutping: fong1 cyun1; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: hong-chhoan).
lead
Originally cast during the Warring States period, these coins continued to be used for the entirety of Imperial China.
lead
The last Chinese cash coins were cast in the first year of the Republic of China.
lead
Generally most cash coins were made from copper or bronze alloys, with iron, lead, and zinc coins occasionally used less often throughout Chinese history.
lead
Rare silver and gold cash coins were also produced.
lead
During most of their production, cash coins were cast, but during the late Qing dynasty, machine-struck cash coins began to be made.
lead

As the cash coins produced over Chinese history were similar, thousand year old cash coins produced during the Northern Song dynasty continued to circulate as valid currency well into the early twentieth century.
lead
In the modern era, these coins are considered to be Chinese "good luck coins"; they are hung on strings and round the necks of children, or over the beds of sick people.
Terminology
There are a variety of Chinese terms for cash coins, usually descriptive and most commonly including the character qián (Chinese: 錢; pinyin: qián) meaning "money".
Ancient China
Around 1200 BC, smaller token spades, hoes, and knives began to be used to conduct smaller exchanges with the tokens later melted down to produce real farm implements.
Qin to Sui dynasties

As standard circular coins were developed following the unification of China by Qin Shi Huang, the most common formation was the round-shaped copper coin with a square or circular hole in the center, the prototypical cash.
Qin to Sui dynasties
The number of coins in a string of cash (simplified Chinese: 一贯钱; traditional Chinese: 一貫錢; pinyin: yīguànqián) varied over time and place but was nominally 1000.
Qin to Sui dynasties
A tael of pure silver in sycee form traded for a fluctuating price of approximately 1000 cash.
Qin to Sui dynasties
A string of cash was divided into ten sections of 100 cash each.
Qin to Sui dynasties
Thus a string of cash could contain 970 coins in one city and 990 in the next.
Qin to Sui dynasties
In some places in the North of China short of currency the custom counted one cash as two and fewer than 500 cash would be exchanged for an ounce of silver.
Qin to Sui dynasties
130 ff.) Paper money equivalents known as flying cash sometimes showed pictures of the appropriate number of cash coins strung together.
Qin to Sui dynasties
Following the Ban Liang cash coins the Han dynasty introduced the San Zhu cash coins which in the year 118 BC were replaced by the Wu Zhu cash coins.
Qin to Sui dynasties
Minting was definitively ended in 618 with the establishment of the Tang dynasty.
Qin to Sui dynasties
Wu Zhu cash coins were cast from 118 BC to 618 AD having a span of 736 years, which is the longest for any coin in human history.
Tang to Qing dynasties
Chinese cash coins were usually made from copper-alloys throughout most of Chinese history, before 1505 they were typically made from bronze and from 1505 onwards they were mostly made from brass.
Tang to Qing dynasties

The last Chinese cash coins were struck, not cast, during the reigns of the Qing Guangxu and Xuantong Emperors shortly before the fall of the Empire in 1911, though even after the fall of the Qing dynasty production briefly continued under the Republic of China.
Cash coins after the fall of the empire
After the fall of the Qing empire, local production of cash coins continued, including the " Minguo Tongbao " (民國通寶) coins in 1912, but were phased out in favour of the new Yuan -based coins.
Cash coins after the fall of the empire

During Yuan Shikai 's brief attempt at monarchy as the Empire of China, trial cash coins are reported to have been minted as part of the "Hong Xiang Tong Bao" (洪憲通寶) series in 1916 but not circulated.
Cash coins after the fall of the empire
During the Republican period cash coins with the inscription Fujian Tongbao (福建通寶) were produced in Fujian, these had the denominations of 1 wén and 2 wén.
Cash coins after the fall of the empire

Trial coins with Fujian Sheng Zao (Chinese: 福建省造), Min Sheng Tong Yong (traditional Chinese: 閩省通用; simplified Chinese: 闽省通用), and a Fujian Tong Bao with a reverse inscribed with Er Wen Sheng Zao (Chinese: 二文省造) were also cast, but never circulated.
Cash coins after the fall of the empire
The coin continued to be used unofficially in China until the mid-20th century.
Cash coins after the fall of the empire
Vietnamese cash coins continued to be cast up until the early 1940s.
Cash coins after the fall of the empire
The last Chinese cash coins in Indonesia circulated in Bali until 1970 and are still used for most Hindu rituals today.
Manufacture
In the mid-19th century, the coins were made of 3 parts copper and 2 parts lead.
Manufacture
Cast silver coins were periodically produced but considerably more rare.
Manufacture
Cast gold coins are also known to exist but are extremely rare.
Early methods of casting

During the Zhou dynasty period, the method for casting coins consisted of first carving the individual characters of a coin together with its general outline into a mould made of either soapstone or clay.
Later methods of manufacture
From the 6th century AD and later, new "mother coins" (mǔ qián 母錢) were cast as the basis for coin production.
Later methods of manufacture
After the metal had cooled down, the "coin tree" (qián shù 錢樹) was extracted from the mould (which would be destroyed due to the process).
Later methods of manufacture
From 1730 during the Qing dynasty, the mother coins were no longer carved separately but derived from "ancestor coins" (zǔ qián 祖錢).
Machine-struck coinage

During the late Qing dynasty under the reign of the Guangxu Emperor in the mid 19th century the first machine-struck cash coins were produced, from 1889 a machine operated mint in Guangzhou, Guangdong opened where the majority of the machine-struck cash would be produced.
Machine-struck coinage
Another effect of the contemporary copper shortages was that the Qing government started importing Korean 5 fun coins and overstruck them with "10 cash".
Inscriptions and denominations
The most common denominations were the ½ tael (Chinese: 半兩; pinyin: bànliǎng) and the 5 zhū (Chinese: 五銖; pinyin: wǔ zhū) coins, the latter being the most common coin denomination in Chinese history.
Inscriptions and denominations

From the Jin until the Tang dynasty the term wén (文), however the term wén which is often translated into English as cash kept being used as an accounting unit for banknotes and later on larger copper coins to measure how many cash coins it was worth.
Inscriptions and denominations
In AD 666, a new system of weights came into effect with the zhū being replaced by the mace (qián) with 10 mace equal to one tael.
Inscriptions and denominations
Coins of the Qing Dynasty (1644–1911) generally carried the era name of the emperor and tongbao on the obverse and the mint location where the coins were cast in Manchu and Chinese on the reverse.
Cash coins and superstitions

In imperial China cash coins were used for fortune telling, or divination, this would be done by first lighting incense to the effigy of a Chinese deity, and then casting three cash coins into a tortoise shell.
Cash coins and superstitions

After this a very intricate system based on the position of the coins with Bagua, and the five elements was used for divination, the Tang dynasty Kai Yuan Tong Bao (開元通寶) coin was the most preferred for this usage.
Cash coins and superstitions

Though in general any cash coin could be used in traditional Chinese medicine, the Kai Yuan Tong Bao was most preferred, and preferences were given for some specific coins for certain ailments E.g. the Zhou Yuan Tong Bao (周元通寶) was used against miscarriages.
Cash coins and superstitions
And Vietnamese cash coins, which have the highest levels of zinc of any cash coins, were ground up into zinc powder that was mixed into either an aqueous solution or a type of ointment.
Stringing of cash coins

Because the counting and stringing together of cash coins was such a time consuming task people known as qiánpù (錢鋪) would string cash coins together in strings of 100 coins of which ten would form a single chuàn.
Stringing of cash coins

The number of coins in a single string was locally determined as in one district a string could consist of 980 cash coins, while in another district this could only be 965 cash coins, these numbers were based on the local salaries of the qiánpù.
Cash coins with flower (rosette) holes
If the shape of these holes were only hexagonal then they were referred to as "turtle shell hole coins" (龜甲穿錢), in some occidental sources they may be called "star holes" because they resemble stars.
Cash coins with flower (rosette) holes
Only a few cash coins produced by the Jurchen -led Jin dynasty are known to have "flower holes".
Cash coins with flower (rosette) holes

During the Ming dynasty period "flower holes" were still (rarely) recoded in Hongwu Tongbao (洪武通寶) and Yongle Tongbao (永樂通寶) cash coins, with the Chongzhen Tongbao (崇禎通寶) series being the last recorded known cash coins to have "flower holes".
Red cash coins
"Red cash coins" (Traditional Chinese: 紅錢) are the cash coins produced in Xinjiang under Qing rule following the conquest of the Dzungar Khanate by the Manchus in 1757.
Red cash coins

In July 1759 General Zhao Hui petitioned to the Qianlong Emperor to reclaim the old pūl coins and using them as scrap for the production of new cash coins, these "red cash coins" had an official exchange rate with the pūl coins that remained in circulation of 1 "red cash" for 2 pūl coins.
Red cash coins
As Zhao Hui wanted the new can coins to have the same weight as pūl coins they weighed 2 qián and had both a higher width and thickness than regular cash coins.
Red cash coins

At the introduction of red cash system in Southern Xinjiang in 1760, the exchange rate of standard cash (or "yellow cash") and "red cash" was set at 10 standard cash coins were worth 1 "red cash coin".
Red cash coins
During two or three subsequent years this exchange rate was decreased to 5:1.
Non-copper-alloy cash coins
During most of their history the cast cash coins of China were predominantly made from bronze or other copper-alloys such as brass.
Non-copper-alloy cash coins
2 iron cash coins were usually worth only a single bronze cash coin.
Non-copper-alloy cash coins
In some cases the usage of certain types of materials to produce cash coins are only more recently discovered due to the lack of historical records mentioning them.
Non-copper-alloy cash coins
For example, it has only been since more recent times that the fact that the Song dynasty had attempted to produce lead cash coins been discovered.
Non-copper-alloy cash coins
Lead cash coins have only been produced at a few times in the monetary history of china, mainly during the Five dynasties and Ten kingdoms period.
Non-copper-alloy cash coins
Because of how soft lead is, most lead cash coins that are found today tend to be very worn.
Usage among overseas Chinese

Usage among overseas Chinese

Usage among overseas Chinese

Not all Chinese cash coins found overseas were brought there by Chinese people, as they were inexpensive to purchase; before 1820, a foreign merchant could buy 1000 cash coins in China for one tael (36 grams) of silver; after 1845, this amount of silver could purchase 2200 or more cash coins.
Usage among overseas Chinese
European merchants started purchasing cash coins in large quantities following the currency reforms enacted by the Ming dynasty between 1570 and 1580.

Akin further cited a number of interviews with elderly Chinese residents of Locke who all claimed that they have never heard of anyone using cash coins as a type of currency there.
